body.input: But ultimately, you should listen to others and empathize with the experience of others and put more love out there in the world.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Now, that hopefully is the way to reduce conflict, reduce violence and reduce that whole psychological experience of being powerless in this world, powerless to become the best version of yourself.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Well, no one's going to disagree with all those fine sentiments, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Yes. But that's an actionable thing is actually practice empathy, right? Like saying that somebody should be silenced or just like this group is bad and this group is good.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: I just feel like that's not empathy. Empathy is understanding the experience of others and respecting it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: I mean, that's what a better world looks like. That's what the reduction of conflict looks like.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: It's like as opposed to saying my tribe is right, your tribe is wrong. Forget the violence and non-violence part.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: That just that act of saying my tribe is right, that tribe is wrong, removing that from the picture.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: That's the way to make a better world. That's the way to reduce the violence, I think.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Not necessarily removing the people who are causing the violence. You have to get to the source of the problem.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: I don't mean the evolutionary source, but just the mindset that creates the violence is usually just lack of empathy for others.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Yeah, but you know, when you can't just teach that because our evolutionary psychology puts us in particular directions.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: So you don't think, do you think it's possible to learn through practice to resist the basics of our evolutionary psychology, the basic forces?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Yeah, I mean, lots and lots of training, lots and lots of education can do it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: The famously most peaceful society that anthropologists have recorded involves a tremendous amount of teaching, including some punishment.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: It's a society in Thailand. You have to beat it out of children to make them nice.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Carrot and steak.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: The point is that you do not find societies in which people are spontaneously showing the kinds of behaviors that we would all love them to show.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: It requires work.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: It requires work.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: What is your book titled Goodness Paradox? What are the main ideas in this book?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Well, the paradox is the fact that humans show extremes in relationship to both violence and nonviolence.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And the violence is that we are one of these few animals in which we use coalition reproductive violence to kill members of our own species.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And we do it in large numbers, just like a few other species.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And the nonviolence is where particularly extreme in how repressed we are in terms of reactive violence.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And I told you the story of how we get there.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: So what's so extraordinary about it is that most animals are either high on both or relatively low on both.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: So chimpanzees are high on proactive violence and reactive violence.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Bonobos are less than chimpanzees on both of those, but still hundreds of times more reactively aggressive than humans are.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: What we've done is retain proactive violence being high and got reactive violence really being low.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And so we have these wonderful societies in which we're all so incredibly nice to each other and tolerant and calm and can meet strangers

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: and have no problem about leading to any kind of conflict at the same time as we are one of the worst killing machine species that's ever existed.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: So what's so extraordinary about this is that if you look at the political philosophers of the last few hundred years,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: you've got this fight famously between Thomas Hobbes and Jean-Jacques Rousseau, or literally you've got the fight between their followers.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: So the followers of Hobbes say, well, Hobbes was right because he says that we are naturally violent and you need a Leviathan,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: a central government or a king to be able to suppress the violence.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: So we're naturally horrid and we can learn to be good, whereas Jean-Jacques Rousseau is interpreted as saying the opposite,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: that we are naturally good and it's only when culture intervenes and horrid ideologies come in that we become uncivilized.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And so people have had this endless fight between are we naturally corrupt or are we naturally kind?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And that has gone on for years and it's only in the last two or three decades that anthropologists like Christopher Bohm and Bruce Nouth have said,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: look, it's obvious what the answer is, we are both of these things.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And what is so exciting now is I think we can understand why we are both.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And the answer is we come from ancestors that were elevated on proactive aggression,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: that were hunters and killers, both of animals and of each other.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And you've got to include that as almost certain from the past.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And then now we've taken our reactive aggression and we've down-regulated it and that's given us power.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: It's given us power because once you get rid of the alpha male, once the beta males take over and force selection in favor of a more tolerant,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: less reactively aggressive individual, the effect is that our cultures suddenly become capable of focusing on things other than conflict.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And so we have social groups in which individuals, instead of constantly being on edge in the way that chimpanzees are with each other,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: are able to interact in ways that enable them to share looking at a tool together or share their food together or pass ideas from one to the other

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: or support each other when they're ill or whatever the issue is, cooperate in ways that make the group far more effective.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: So you asked earlier, what did I think about why sapiens was able to expand at the expense of Neanderthals so dramatically around 40,000 years ago?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And the answer is that whatever it was, it had something to do with the sapiens' ability to cooperate.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: That was what gave them bigger groups. That's what enabled them to have a far more effective way of living.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And I suspect it was to do with weapons and military aspects. But even if it wasn't that,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: the greater cooperation that sapiens were showing would have been hugely important.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: So sapiens then had groups of, who knows exactly how big they were, but scores of people to judge from their remains.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Whereas Neanderthals were living in widely separated small groups of maybe as many as 15 or 20 people sometimes,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: where they saw others so rarely that they were inbreeding at high levels.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Fathers having babies with their daughters. Very different world.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Very different world.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And that's probably what our world was like before we got sapiens.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Before we got sapiens. And it's fascinating that there was that kind of violence against...

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Once you get rid of the alpha males, you have now the freedom to have kindness amongst the beta males.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Not kindness, but collaboration. That's the better word.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Yes. Much more cooperation. Not just among the males, but among the beta males, but also among the gamma males and the females.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Yeah. I don't know what a gamma male is, but I imagine there's a whole alphabet.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Well, I don't know about a whole alphabet, but I think the big layers are the married men and the unmarried men.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Because the married men had a problem with the unmarried men.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: You see it in ethnographies of hunters and gatherers recently, where the unmarried men would be given rules.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Such as, a very extreme rule in Northern Australia was you cannot come to the camp for months.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: You have to go away and live somewhere out in the bush.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Yes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Because we don't want you anywhere near our wives.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And then another kind of rule is if you are in the camp, you must be in the firelight all the time.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Otherwise, we don't know what you're doing out in the dark.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: So you really have us to control them, because the men who had lots of wives did not want those horrid bachelor sneaking around the place.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: I love this.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: You also wrote the book titled Catching Fire, How Cooking Made Us Human.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: What's the central idea in this book?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: The subtitle, How Cooking Made Us Human, refers not to homo sapiens, but to homo erectus.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: So human there means the genus homo.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And homo erectus is the first full member of the genus homo in the sense that it looked like us, just with a slightly more robust build and a smaller brain.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And the central idea of Catching Fire is that it was the control of fire that was responsible for the emergence of homo erectus and therefore the genus homo,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: which happened two million years ago.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And it was an evolution from a line of australopithecines.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And australopithecines are the creatures from whom we evolved.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: They were present in Africa from something like six or seven million years ago, up to actually up to one million years ago.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And then a branch led off to homo around two million years ago.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And the way to think of australopithecines is that they were like chimpanzees standing upright.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: So they were erect bipedal walkers.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: They were like chimpanzees in the sense that they had brains about the size of a chimpanzee.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: They were literally about the body size of a chimpanzee, a little bit smaller, actually.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And they had big jaws because they were still eating raw food.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: They had big teeth and big jaws.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And then around two million years ago, the line of australopithecines, which ended with an intermediate species, a kind of missing link area,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: because it is not missing, called habilis, sometimes called homo habilis, but more properly in my view called australopithecus habilis.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: That gave rise to homo erectus.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And homo erectus, here's how different it was.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: It had a smaller mouth, a smaller jaw, smaller teeth, and to judge from its ribs and pelvis, smaller gut.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: In addition, it had lost what australopithecines all had, which was adaptations for climbing in the trees.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And that meant that homo erectus must have slept on the ground.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And since it slept on the ground, it should have been able to defend itself somehow against predators.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And I can't think of any way they could have done that unless they had fire.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: So there are two major clues to why it was with homo erectus that our ancestors first acquired the control of fire.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: One is the fact that they were clearly not sleeping in trees in the way that chimpanzees and gorillas and bonobos and all the other primates do.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And the other is that there was this striking reduction throughout the gut, reduction in size of the mouth and the chewing apparatus and in the gut itself.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And that conforms to what we see nowadays about humans, which is that our guts are about two thirds of the size of what they would be if we ate raw food to judge by the great apes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: So at some point in our evolution, we acquired the skill of cooking and skill of controlling fire.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: At no time between two million years ago and the present, do we see any changes in our anatomy that can, as it were, justify the enormous change that happens when you are an animal that learns to control fire.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: But at two million years ago, we have exactly what you'd expect.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Namely, the guts becoming smaller because the food is becoming softer and much more easy to digest. So you don't have to work so hard in your body to digest it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And as I say, a commitment to sleeping on the ground, which I think you'd be absolutely crazy to do nowadays on a moonless night in the middle of Serengeti unless you had fire.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: I've slept out quite a lot in various parts of Africa in the bush, and you will not catch me just lying on the ground in an area with lots of predators unless I got a fire with me.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: You're going to get eaten.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: You're going to get terrified and you're going to get eaten.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Okay. So there's a million questions I want to ask. So one is it's very naturally coupled, the discovery of controlled fire and cooking with fire. Is that an obvious leap?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Well, here's what we know. We know that all the animals that we've tested like to eat their food cooked more than they like it raw.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Okay.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: So this is true for all the great apes. We've tested them.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: That's fascinating, by the way. Why is that? That's just like a property of food, I suppose.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Yes, I think what it is is that animals are always looking for any kind of way to get food that is easier to digest.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And there are various signals in the food, such as the amount of sugar there, the amount of free amino acids, because the amino acids can be tasted.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And the physical qualities of the food be particularly important, how tough the food is. Always prefer softer food, provided it feels safe, tastes safe.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And these kinds of sensory cues are all there in cooked food. It's soft. It doesn't have so many toxins. It's not so noxious to taste, easier to chew.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: So everyone loves it spontaneously. Your dogs and your cats prefer cooked food to raw food.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Well, maybe you can say that's a consequence of domestication. But even, as I say, all of the great apes, you test naive ones and they prefer it cooked if they can.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: So then, obviously, once you have fire, you're going to accidentally discover that food changes when you apply fire to it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And then it's going to be the big, crazy new fad.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: You took the words out of my mouth. I mean, if they have fire at all and their food rolls into it, five minutes later, it tastes better than it did before.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: How big of an invention from an engineering perspective do you think is the discovery of fire?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Do you think for the homo erectus, homo sapiens, do you think it's the greatest invention ever?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Yeah, I think that the control of fire has been ultimately responsible for essentially how grandiose do I want to be here.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: The entire human story, going back to homo, is what changed us from being a regular kind of animal.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And perhaps the biggest way in which it is likely to have changed us is it reduced the difficulty of making a large brain.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: So the story here is that the constraints on brain size are energetic.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: You and I have brains that are something like 2.5% of our body weight.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: It consumes around 25% of all of our calories. So it's disproportionate.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: There are other expensive organs in our bodies as well, such as the heart.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And what's different about the brain is that in addition to us being able to fuel it in a way that other animals can't,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: we also have reasons for wanting to have an even bigger brain, whereas we don't want an even bigger heart.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: So what those reasons are is unclear.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: With regard to the costs of maintaining a brain, cooking makes it possible because it's supplying more calories,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: and it is enormously reducing the amount of time that it takes to chew your food.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: So if you were a gorilla and you wanted to have a bigger brain, you might say, okay, well, let's just eat some more.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: But gorillas are eating for pretty much the entire day in the sense that they're eating for maybe seven or eight hours a day in some seasons.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: That's just chewing. And then they've got to sit around and digest their food because they can't just eat all the time.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: They've got to take a break while the food is digested in the stomach and then passed into the gut.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: So the stomach is already full. So basically gorillas are eating at about the maximum rate already.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: So how does a gorilla get a bigger brain? It doesn't.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: It's actually got a smaller brain relative to its body size than a chimpanzee does.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And that's the basic problem for our ancestors.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Then you come along and cook, and all of a sudden you can get an increased amount of energy from your food.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: You are spending much less energy on digesting your food.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: There are 25 bodily processes or more that are involved in digesting your food, making the acid that takes the proteins apart,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: maintaining the brush border where the molecules are taken across the gut wall, and so on.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: That all costs. It costs you to digest your food. It costs less if you cook your food.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: So you get a net gain in the amount of energy.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And you are reducing the amount of time from, in the case of our ancestors, probably around 50% of the day chewing,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: to nowadays one hour a day chewing. So all of a sudden you've got hours a day in which to do other things,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: to use those brains that you've now enabled to grow.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: So with Homo rectus, you start the process of getting a bigger brain and famously, you know,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: throughout the whole period of the evolution of the genus Homo, you have a steadily increasing size of brain

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: until right at the end when it actually gets smaller, but that's a different story.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Which end is this? Are we talking about Homo sapiens?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Yeah. With Homo sapiens, you've got a smaller brain from people who haven't got it exactly down,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: but at least 30,000 years ago, it starts declining.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And so the fascinating thing about that is that all domesticated animals have smaller brains than their wild ancestors.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And I...

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: The domestication is intricately connected to this brain size, you think?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Exactly. So I think what we're seeing in humans is that same manifestation.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And then the fascinating question is why?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And the only point I would want to make about this is that there is no evidence that in the small brain domesticates,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: they're losing, say, an average of about 15% of brain size.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: In the small brain domesticates compared to their wild ancestors, there's no indication of a loss of cognitive ability.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: So I think what's going on is that it's a younger brain.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: It's a more pedomorphic brain, looking like the juveniles of the ancestor.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: But just as our kids are very smart and can learn amazing things compared to adults, all they lack is wisdom and maturity.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: But in terms of sheer cognitive ability, they got it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And I think that's the same with domesticated animals compared to their wild ancestors.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And probably, therefore, with Homo sapiens, say, 30,000 years ago, compared to their ancestors.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: So we have smaller brains than the undertiles.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Size, Richard, isn't everything.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Exactly.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: What's the connection between fire cooking and the eating of meat?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Which came first, do you think?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Do you think humans starting to enjoy the eating of meat or the invention of fire and the use of fire for cooking?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: I think that fire increased the use of meat.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: But the fact that chimpanzees really like to hunt and kill meat, as do bonobos, certainly puts us in...

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: So those two species have a common ancestor with us going six, seven million years ago.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And it was from that common ancestor that you get the Australopithecine line.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: It's very likely, therefore, Australopithecines were eating meat when they could get it, which wouldn't be very often because they wouldn't be very good sprinters.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: But nevertheless, they would occasionally be able to get some meat.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And I bet they loved it all the time.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And basically, all primates like meat if they can get it, almost all of them.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: But I think fire would have been very important for a couple of reasons.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: One is that once you eat your food cooked, then you're saving yourself time.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: By saving yourself time, you can free up the opportunity to go and hunt more.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Because hunting is a high-risk, high-gain activity.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: There's every risk that you will get nothing on one particular afternoon that you go off looking for opportunities to kill.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: But it's high gain because when you do get something, you bring down a kudu, then you've got a serious amount of meat.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: What did males and females do with the time they were saving from not having to chew their food?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: I think that in the case of males, it's very reasonable to think they spent a greatly increased amount of time hunting.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: So chimpanzees, they hunt maybe two or three times a month, and the average hunt length is 20 minutes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: With humans, they're hunting maybe 20 times a month, and the average hunt length is six hours.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: So it's a huge difference.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And that's possible because the time was available because they were cooking.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Less chewing, more hunting.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: You got it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: The other thing is that the meat is so much nicer.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: So when a chimpanzee kills a monkey, and they are so excited about killing a monkey.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: They are so excited about going into the hunt, and when they make the kill, then there's screams everywhere.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And some try to seize it and capture it and take it away from the others.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And eventually the strongest one has it, and the others sit around begging and trying to get some and tear it off.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And so they all love it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: There are others who he often goes to the top of a tree in order to be able to get away from all of these beggars and scavengers.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And while he's there, drops of blood or little scraps fall down to the bottom.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And the junior members of society, the females and young and that sort of thing,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: they are racing through to find a particular leaf that's got a drop of blood on it so they can lick it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: I mean, they love it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: But it takes them a lot of time to chew it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: I mean, it's the same thing as for cooked food in general.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: So they are getting meat very slowly into their bodies.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And there sometimes comes a time when they just say, I've had enough of this.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: I need real food. And they'll drop the meat and go off and eat fruit again,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: because they can get fruit into their bodies so much faster than they can get meat.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: So once they're cooking, that problem is solved and they can eat the meat much more readily.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: So I think that meat eating would become important for two reasons with cooking.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: So the key, not to oversimplify, but the key moments in human history are with the Homo erectus,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: the discovery of fire and the use of fire for cooking.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And then with Homo sapiens, the beta males killing off the alpha males so that the cooperation can exist.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And cooperation leads to communication and language and ideas, the sharing of ideas, that kind of thing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Well, yes, the only thing I would modify on that is that you have to ask,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: how is it that the beta males were able to kill the alpha male?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And we now know that although chimpanzees do kill males within their own group sometimes,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: it's not a process of killing the alpha male.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: It's taking advantage of opportunity when some male gets into a bad position,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: but it's not a systematic ability to kill the alpha male.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And you can see why, because they don't have language.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And without language, it's very difficult to know how confident you can be of the support of others

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: against a particular individual within your own group.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: When you're attacking someone from another group, that problem is solved.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: We all hate those guys.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: But the alpha male has got alliances within his group.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Some of those allies might be willing to turn against him.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Some of them might be harboring deep feelings of resentment.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: But how does anyone else know that?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: So in other words, I think that you have to have some kind of language that is pretty good

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: to solve the problems of gaining confidence that five of you say, you know, or some number,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: can trust each other in this final attack.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And even nowadays, it's difficult.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: You mentioned Stalin.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: It's like, why was everybody terrified?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Any dictator that takes control.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Why is all of us as individuals terrified when you know there's millions of us?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: That's right.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And so like that, we lack the language because our basic psychology of fear overtakes us.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Like who can we talk to?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Who can we talk to and not get killed ourselves?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Exactly. That's right.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: But do you have this intuition that some kind of language was developing along with this process of beta males taking over?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Yes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: I mean, once you have sufficient language to be able to have the beta males conspiring to kill the alpha male,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: then you have selection in favor of cooperation and tolerance, as we spoke about.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And at that point, there will be increased ability to communicate and the language will get richer and better and better.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: So yes, absolutely.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Positive feedback loop once you get the situation started.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Can you maybe comment on the full complexity and richness of the human mind through this process?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: We've been casually saying cooking, fire and beta males leading to cooperation.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: But how does the beauty of the human mind emerge from all of this?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Is there other further steps we need to understand?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Or is it as simple as this language emerging from taking over the alpha male and the cooperation?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Or am I also over romanticizing how amazing the human mind is?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Is it just like one small step in a long journey of evolution?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Well, if the beauty of the human mind is the ability of us all to be creative, to explore, that's one kind of beauty.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Another kind of beauty is the empathy that we can show and we think of that as beautiful because it is a kind of rare and special ability

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: compared to the sort of ordinary selfishness that can commonly predominate.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: I suppose we have to think of different sources for those two types.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: I suppose a general answer is that there has been selection in favor of bigger brains,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: which probably in general has been associated with increasing cognitive ability.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: As that has happened, the complexity of life has increased because people have more and more complex,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: highly differentiated strategies in response to each other's more complex, highly differentiated strategies.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: We get to a point where there is deception and self-deception.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: There is a manipulation of ideas through stories that we invent and stories that we pass on.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: I guess all I'm wanting to say is that there is a world of the mind that evolves in response to these platforms that are put there,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: the platform of increasing brain size and therefore cognitive ability made possible by increased energy supply,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: the platform of cooperation and tolerance in a world in which there remains a lot of conflict

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: and therefore a need to respond to the conflict and manipulate your allies appropriately.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: I don't see beauty as coming, either kind of beauty, as coming sort of totally independently of these things.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: I don't think there's a selection for staring into the sunset and creating poetry.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: But I guess sexual selection, males wanting to impress females in different ways will lead to them wanting to-

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Write poetry?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Well, yes, show off.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Yeah, in all the different ways. So all of these are natural consequences of just coming up with strategies of how to cooperate and how to achieve certain ends.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: So that's just like a natural-

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Yeah, I mean, we haven't spoken about sexual selection, but that is a really important part of it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: They try to out-compete each other normally without any physical conflict just in order to be able to be chosen by mates of the opposite sex.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And that is certainly a major source of creativity.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: So you've studied chimps. You also, all the other relatives, gorillas.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: What do you find beautiful and fascinating about chimps, about gorillas, about humans?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Maybe you can paint the whole picture of that evolutionary, that little local pocket of the evolutionary tree.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: How are we related? What is the common ancestor? What are the interesting differences?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: I know I'm asking a million questions, but can you paint a map of what are chimps, gorillas, and humans, like how we're related, and what you find fascinating about each?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: In Africa, straddling the equator, there is a strip of rainforest that relies on the combination of high temperatures and rainfall that you get around the equator.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: That rainforest goes into about 22 countries, and throughout those countries you have chimpanzees, although they've gone extinct in two of them.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: In just a fraction of them, five countries, you've got gorillas, where there are mountains.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And in one country, on the left bank of the Great Congo River, you have bonobos.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: In the African forest, you've got these three African apes, the only African apes, all of which are very similar in much of their way of life.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: They walk on their knuckles through the forest, looking for fruit trees and eating herbs when they can't find fruits.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Gorillas represent the oldest chain.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: So about 10 million years ago, maybe as recently as eight million years ago, the ancestor gorillas broke off from the ancestor leading to chimps and bonobos and humans.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: So they probably remained very similar now to what they were then.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: They were probably the largest apes living in montane areas and spending more time eating just herbs, stems, not so vitally dependent on fruit.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And living in, if it was like the present, groups up to about 50 stable groups with one alpha male who was in charge.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Gorillas are wonderfully slow and inquisitive compared to chimps and bonobos.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: I had the privilege of spending a week or two with gorillas at Diane Fosse's camp before she was murdered.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And I went out with two women, Kelly and Barb, to a particular group.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And there was a young female in the group called Simba, and Simba approached us and stared at the two women.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And then she came towards me and she very deliberately reached out her knuckles and touched me on the forehead.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: She was watched in doing this by a young male who was quite keen on her, and he was called Digit.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And about five minutes later, Digit stood in front of us on the path.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And Kelly was in front of me, and then there was Barb, and then there was me.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And he came charging down the path and he sidestepped around Kelly and he sidestepped around Barb.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And me, he just knocked with his arm and sent me flying about five yards into the bushes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And I loved the way that that was a very deliberate response.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And I loved the way that Simba had been so interested in me and held my eye.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Chimps and bonobos never hold your eye, but gorillas really look as though they're trying to sort of figure out, what are you thinking about?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: That was a species that goes back for something like 10 million years.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: In that situation, was there a game being played?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Well, I mean, I felt that Digit was telling me, I don't want you messing with Simba.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: But was Simba using you?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Oh, I see. Well, that's a fun idea.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: I don't see why she should be using me, but you mean testing how strongly Digit was prepared to intervene to.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Yeah, exactly.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: That's come straight out of a sort of adolescent to high school playbook.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: You're right.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Well, that's all.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: No, no, no. There's nothing wrong with it for that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: I never thought of that and you never know.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: So, yeah. So, okay. So this is an ancient branch of the evolutionary tree that led to gorillas.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: So then the next thing that happened on the evolutionary tree was six or seven million years ago when you have the line between chimps and bonobos on the one hand and humans on the other splitting.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And basically what happened is that at that point, a chimp-like ancestor leaves the forest, gets isolated in an area outside the forest and adapts, and that becomes the Australopithecines.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And meanwhile, the chimpanzees and bonobo ancestor continues in the forest.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And later what happens is that one branch of that crosses the Congo River and becomes the bonobos.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: That was only about two million years ago, maybe one million years ago.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Now, the chimps that remained in the forest throughout this time and occupied all the countries across from West to East Africa now,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: again, we assume that they're pretty similar to the ones that live nowadays, where there's some variation from West to East.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And these are animals that live in social communities of between, say, 20 and 200.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: They have a lot of them in one group, but they never come together in a single unit.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: They share an area, a community territory, and that area is defended by males, and within it, females wander and bring up their young independently.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And the females are very scared about the possibility that males will be mean to their infants.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And in order to avoid them doing that, they do their best to mate with every single male in the group multiple times as if to give a memory in that male of,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: yeah, yeah, I remitted you, so I'm not going to be mean to your baby.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: So what's wonderful about chimps? Well, as we've spoken about them, they are creative and amazingly human-like.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: But I love the sort of, you know, the quiet moments. And here's one.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: I've got two chimps who are grooming each other on a day when they are utterly exhausted.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: They've walked 11 kilometers the day before, up and down hills.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And on this particular day, all they do is they get to one tree and they eat from that tree.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And other than that, they only walk about 100 yards and they go back to sleep in the nest in which they woke up.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: So they're utterly exhausted and they're just eating nonstop because they're trying to recover their energy.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And this is Hugh and Charlie. And we think they were probably brothers, though we never actually got the genetic evidence to prove it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Well, I never remember now who it is, but let's say that they both come down from the tree

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: and they're both carrying branches of the food, they're actually seeds from these branches.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: They're both engaged even in the midday sun when they want to come down and unshade themselves for a bit on the ground, they're still eating.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: But then Charlie finishes his branch and he starts grooming Hugh.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And Hugh continues eating from his branch.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Charlie eventually gets bored of this after a few minutes and he reaches out and he lifts the branch from which Hugh is still taking seeds

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: and puts it over his head and puts it behind his back as far as possible away from Hugh.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Hugh doesn't do anything. He just finishes his mouthful and then he turns to Charlie and grooms him.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: So this very polite way of saying, will you groom me please, has worked.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229
