body.input: Then Hugh grooms around Charlie's back and around to the right side and then down his arm to what point where he can reach the branch again.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And then he picks up the branch and continues.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Nonchalantly.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Right. So in other words, a very simple little strategy, but it just shows the courtesy with which they can treat each other.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And the days I love with chimps, when you see that sort of thing or when you see mothers just lying in a sunlit patch in the forest

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: with babies bouncing on top of them, just having a wonderful peaceful time.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And that's what most of their lives are like.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: So chimpanzees are the species that kind of unites the rest of the apes because a gorilla is in many ways just a big version of a chimpanzee.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: If you can sort of engineer a chimpanzee in your mind to be bigger, it basically turns into a gorilla.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And then bonobos on the left bank of the Congo River are like a domesticated form of a chimpanzee.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: But obviously humans didn't domesticate them, so they're self-domesticated.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: They are less aggressive and they show all the marks of domestication that domestication animals do compared to wild animals in their bones.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: So they have reduced differences between males and females in which the males are more like females.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: They have smaller brains. They have shorter faces, smaller teeth and smaller bodies.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: All the things that domesticated animals show.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And bonobos live in this environment in a strikingly peaceful way compared to the chimpanzees.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: There's no indication that they will have these aggressive kills and enough data now to show that there's a statistical difference in the frequency in which it would happen.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And bonobos are famously erotic.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: The females have enlarged sexual parts, which swell to particularly large size compared to the female chimpanzees.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And the females have a lot of interactions with each other in which they excitedly rub their clitorises together and appear to have orgasms.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And these occur in the context of some kind of social tension.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And they sometimes happen before, sometimes happen after the social tension, and they seem to be devices, these interactions, for ensuring that everyone's friends and reducing the chances that they're actually going to get into a fight.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: So it's a kind of conflict resolution through sex or some kind of pleasurable sexual experience.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Well, it's often characterized as make love, not war.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Make love, not war.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Okay.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: You mentioned to me offline that you have a deep love for nature.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: If we look at the world today, how can we ensure that the beautiful parts of nature remain a big part of our lives as human beings?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: In the way we think about it, in the way we also keep it around, preserve it, you know, we keep it part of our minds and part of our world.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: It's a very difficult question because every time there is a conflict between conservation of a natural habitat and allowing people to get that little bit of extra food for their babies, then naturally the tendency is for the humans to win.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: So we have this steady erosion in the face of tremendous efforts to conserve nature.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: We have a continuing steady erosion of habitats and all the species, and the numbers are always in the wrong direction.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Occasionally you get sort of wonderful little examples of something being saved, but the overall trend is clear.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And it's very difficult to see how one can ever escape that because it's not human, now that we are essentially a single tribe, to want to save an elephant if it means killing 20 humans.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: So I think the only way in which we can really conserve is if we put tremendous effort into conserving the very best representative areas of nature.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Often this will be the national parks that already exist, and what we have to do is to make them so valuable that actually it is worth it in terms of human survival to be able to keep those sorts of places.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And that's the attitude that my colleagues and I have taken in Uganda, where we want to keep the Kibale National Park alive, which has got the largest population of chimpanzees in Uganda, and it's got elephants and wonderful birds and wonderful butterflies and wonderful plants and so on, and visitors.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Lots and lots of visitors. It may be that we're going to have to have huge increases in the amount of charges that you pay for ecotourism, and you need to make sure that ecotourism is done right.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: In other places, you will keep nature there because it's useful for maintaining the climate, bringing rain. Maybe you can in some places convince people of the sheer aesthetics of keeping nature that even over the long term,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: presidents whose job it is to look for the future of the country will be persuaded that you can do it for purely aesthetic reasons.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: But overall, what is required is for people in the rich countries to do much more investment than they have so far in maintaining both the natural places in their own countries and in the tropics.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: If you look at Africa, the population trends are that Nigeria may become the most populous country in the world, I think, within a century.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: The future of African habitats, it's clear what's going to happen in general. There's going to be a huge conversion towards agricultural land.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: I heard Ed Wilson speak years ago about the prospect of the entire globe being turned into a single human feedlot.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: It's going to take a lot to avoid that. He is out there calling for half the earth to be devoted to nature.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: It's incredibly ambitious and incredibly optimistic. But unless you have really exciting goals, probably nothing will be achieved.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Yeah, I mean, there's something to me, like when I visit New York and I see Central Park and then somehow we constructed a situation where you preserve this park in the middle, probably some of the most expensive land in the world.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: The fact that that's possible gives me hope that you can do this kind of preservation at a global scale, perhaps for just the aesthetic reasons of just valuing the beauty and just respecting our origins of having come from the earth.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: We are so incredibly lucky to have chimpanzees, bonobos, and gorillas as our close relatives still living on the earth. We're unlucky that we don't have Australopithecines and other species of Homo, but we're still lucky to have those because they are incredibly closely related to us compared to what most animals have.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: There are many animals that don't have any close relatives to them on the earth, but not only are they relatively close, but they teach us so much about ourselves.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: The similarities between them and ourselves raise questions that we can then test about the extent to which our own behavioral propensities are derived from the same evolutionary stock as in those great apes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Well, how much is that worth? We could spend billions going to the Mars to find evidence of bacteria there, and that's fascinating too.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: But we should be spending billions on this earth in order to make sure that we have substantial representative populations of these close relatives.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Yeah, that we can meet. There's something like space tourism. When you go out into space and you look back down on earth, that's to a lot of people, including myself, is worth a lot.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: But why is that worth a lot? It's because it's humbling and beautiful in the same way that meeting our close evolutionary relatives is humbling and beautiful.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Just to know that this is what we come from. This is who we are. Not just for the understanding or the science of it, but just something about the beauty of witnessing this.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Again, it's both humbling and empowering that this place is fragile and we're damn lucky to be here.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Yes. Unfortunately, the problems are incredibly difficult to solve and there is no one solver. It has to happen from a network of potentially cooperating people.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: But you're so right about it being daunting to think about what it looks like from space.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: I love the view that Herman Muller expressed of being able to go out from space and he said the whole of life would look like a kind of rust on the planet.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Yeah, so the aliens were to visit. I'm not sure they would notice the life. They would probably notice the trees or ocean. It's a kind of rust.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: But let me ask the big ridiculous philosophical question. What is the meaning of this rust? What do you think is the meaning of life on Earth? What is the meaning of our human intelligent life?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Well, I think it's very clear that we have an evolutionary story that is only getting challenged around the edges.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: We have a very clear understanding of the evolution of life and the meaning is we are here as a consequence of materialistic processes that began in our sense with the establishment of the Earth

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: four and a half billion years ago, wherever it was, and then water and oxygen and so on. And we are the astonishing consequence of the evolution of cells and multicellular organisms.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: The word random is the wrong word to use unless you understand what it means. It didn't happen by chance, but a lot of random events had to happen to make this possible.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And those random events, of course, are the production of appropriate mutations. But the meaning of life is there is no meaning.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: The really big mystery of life is why is there a universe?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And that same why propagates itself through the whole of it, through the whole process of it for the emergence of planets, the emergence, first of all, of galaxies, of star systems, of planets,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: of the proteins required to construct the single cell organisms and the single cell organism becoming complex organisms and some of the clever fish crawling out onto the land and the whole of it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And then there's fire, some clever guy or lady invented fire, and then now here we are. It just does seem, speaking as a human, kind of special that we're able to reflect on the whole thing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Wonderful story. It's so much more interesting than the stories produced by religion.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: It is beautiful, but it just seems special that us humans are able to write religions and construct stories and also do science.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: That seems kind of amazing. It seems like the universe is such that it creates beings like us that are able to investigate it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And that's why there's this longing for a why. That's such a beautiful little pocket of complexity created by the universe.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: It seems like there should be a why, but maybe there's just an infinite number of universes, and this is the one that led to this particular set of humans.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Even without an infinite number of universes, I bet there's an infinite number of intelligent beings.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Throughout this universe.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Yeah. Now that we know how many planets have the right sort of conditions, which is what? I can't remember, a lot.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: It's some significant percentage of all planets. Then there are apparently billions of planets.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Things happen so quickly on Earth. Once you've got water, then you've got life.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: It did not take long for life to evolve in the big scheme of things.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And if you think you look out there, say there's a nearly infinite number of intelligent civilizations, one dimension you can look at is the proclivity to violence they have.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: It's interesting to think what level of violence is useful for extending the life of a civilization.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: So we have a particular set of violence in our history. Maybe being too peaceful is a problem in the early days.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Maybe being too violent, quite obviously, is a problem.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: So you look at viruses. What kind of viruses on Earth propagate and succeed? If you're too deadly, that's a big problem.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: If you're not deadly enough, that's also a problem. So that is a fascinating exploration of...

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: I don't see any evidence. I don't see where you're coming from when you say that being too peaceful is a problem.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Well, because... I'll say it this way. Death is a way to get rid of suboptimal solutions. So violence...

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: But there's lots of ways to die without violence.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Right. To me, death in itself is violence. And you can... I mean, a lot of people that talk about, for example, longevity and disease and all that kind of stuff, they see death is...

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: This is the way they talk about it. And it's interesting to philosophically think of it that way.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: It's like mass murder that's happening. And it's like people that try to, from a biological perspective, help extend life.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: They see that you're helping... The biggest atrocity in the history of human civilization, from their perspective, is not allocating all our resources to solving death.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Right? Because death is a kind of violence. It is a kind of murder that we're allowing to be committed on us by nature.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And so the flip side of that is death makes way for new life, for new ideas. And so that...

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Yes. But that's got nothing to do with peace versus war. I mean, you have animals that are very, very peaceful, but they evolve just in the same way as other animals do.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: They just don't do it with death caused by violence. And violent death is premature death, surely. I mean, I don't mind about people dying.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: What I mind about is people dying in their youth, middle age.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Prematurally. But some people would say all death is premature. It certainly feels that way. It's died too soon. Anyone who's ever died, died too soon.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Yeah. Well, I mean, if we can become like sequoias and live for hundreds of years and thousands of years, that would be great.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Do you ponder your own mortality? Are you afraid of death?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: I don't think I'm afraid of it. I'm reconciled to the fact it's going to happen. I just feel frustrated because I enjoy life and I don't want to leave the party.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Yeah. It's kind of a fun party. I don't want to leave the party either. So however we got here, we made one heck of an awesome party.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: And you're right. Having a party with a little bit less violence than it is an even more fun party. Richard, I'm deeply honored that you spent time with me today.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Your work is amazing. It includes some of the deepest thinking about our human history and the nature of human civilization. So again, thank you so much for talking today. It's an honor.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Thanks for your great questions. It was a really fun conversation.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Wrangham: Violence, Sex, and Fire in Human Evolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #229

body.input: Thanks for listening to this conversation with Richard Wrangham. To support this podcast, please check out our sponsors in the description.
