metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: The reality is when you do really difficult things, engineering things, all these inventions along the way are created.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: It's kind of fascinating.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: Basically, just pick a thing that everyone can agree is kind of cool and is really hard and do that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And then you'll have like thousands of inventions that have nothing to do with the thing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: That's right.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: I think you should let curious scientists just follow what they're interested in to a certain extent.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: In science, we say we have translational research where we say, okay, here's some money.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: Go cure cancer or diabetes or heart disease, whatever, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And that's fine.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: But that often doesn't work out very well.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: What works better is to say, you have a good lab, you have a good track record, here's some money, do something.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And that's where PCR, CRISPR, recombinant DNA, all that stuff which has made the field explode, that's all it came from.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: Not from people saying, I want to cure genetic diseases by gene editing, but by saying, what are these repeated things in this bacterium doing?

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: Yep. Can I ask you a big philosophical question?

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: So there's these deadly viruses that are not very transmissible, Ebola, rabies.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And then there's these less deadly viruses that are very transmissible, like COVID, I guess kind of borderline.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: But why isn't there super transmissible, super deadly viruses?

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: I think if you compare SARS-1 and 2, you get somewhat of an answer, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: SARS-1 was more deadly.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: In fact, over half of the time when people were infected, they ended up in the hospital because they were that sick.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And then the peak of virus shedding from them happened long after they went in the hospital.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: So it's easy to contain the infection when you're in a hospital, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: There was not much pre-symptomatic or asymptomatic shedding with SARS-1.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And shedding means you become infectious.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: So in a respiratory virus, you inhale the droplets with the virus, and they reproduce in your upper respiratory tract, what we call the nasopharynx, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: The nose and going back to that little cavity just above your mouth.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: So the virus reproduces really well.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And then as you talk and sneeze and cough, you expel droplets, and then those are inhaled by other people.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And then they reproduce.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And for SARS-2, we now know there's a lot of reproduction just before you feel anything, if at all.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: So there's a lot of shedding and transmission before you get symptomatic.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And many people don't ever get symptomatic, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: So they spread really easily.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: So that explains why some viruses can transmit a lot better than others.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And if one happens to knock you out, then you're never going to transmit because you're in the hospital like SARS-1.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: But why can't you have both?

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: Why can't you just wait a while before it knocks you out, but when it knocks you out, it really kills you?

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: That is a philosophical question, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: Because we could talk about why we haven't observed it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: I mean, one issue is that if you're killed too quickly by a highly lethal virus, you're not going to transmit it very well.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: So Ebola can kill you quite rapidly.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And most of the transmission occurs when people are being cared for at home or in hospitals.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: The doctors and nurses get the virus, but people walking around, you're not walking around when you have Ebola.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: You're too sick.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: You have black, bloody diarrhea.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: You're vomiting.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: You're bleeding from your skin and mucous membranes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: You're not walking around.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: You're not going to parties.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: So I think that's part of it, that if the infection is too lethal, you're simply not a good transmitter.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And I think transmission is probably one of the most powerful selection forces for viruses, because a virus always has to find a new host.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: If it doesn't, it's a startup that fails, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: If it doesn't find a new host, it's gone.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And so anything that makes the virus transmit better is going to help it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And if killing you, being less lethal, is part of that, that works too.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: So there's a strong selection pressure against being lethal.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: I think there's a strong selection pressure against being lethal and being more transmissible.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: Those two seem to work in opposite ways.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And now we don't have a lot of data to support this.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: This is kind of a thought experiment.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: But there is one experiment done in Australia many years ago.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: I don't know if you know this, but in the 1800s, the hunters in Australia imported a rabbit from Europe so they could hunt it,

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: because the native rabbit in Australia was too fast for them.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: They couldn't shoot them.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: So they brought in this European rabbit, and they reproduced out of control.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: Within a couple of years, they were everywhere.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: Millions of rabbits in all the watering holes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And now they had a problem.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: So they decided to use a virus to get rid of these excess rabbits.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And they used a virus, a pox virus called myxoma virus, which is a natural virus of a different kind of rabbit.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: But for these European rabbits, it was quite lethal.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And it's spread by mosquitoes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: So they said, OK, let's release this virus.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: In the first year, 99.2% of the rabbits were killed.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: But that 0.8% that were left had some form of resistance.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: They were variants.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: Every organism, not just viruses, makes mutants.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And there were some variants of the rabbits that could survive infection.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And then in subsequent years, the virus became less lethal.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And then the mosquitoes had a better shot of transmitting it from one rabbit to another if the rabbit lived longer.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: That's the selection, probably.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And so in the end, the rabbits lived on.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: The virus was there.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: It evolved to be more transmissible and less lethal.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: So that's the only data.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: Life on Earth is amazing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: It is. It is.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: If you take the time to look at it and see what's happened, it is amazing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: It's also humbling that it just makes you realize humans are just a small part of the picture.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: Of course.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And we're wrecking it, aren't we?

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: Well, I mean, that's not really...

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: I mean, viruses are wrecking it some ways.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: We're not really wrecking anything.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: It's all part of it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: But you know, when the ways that humans exist encourages viruses to infect us, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: When we were hunter-gatherers living in bands of 100 people, very few viruses, because it was hard for the virus to go from one band to another.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And perhaps a hunter would... one of these humans would get an animal and bring a virus into camp, and some people would die, but it would never spread to another.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And then when we started to congregate in cities, we figured out agriculture and so forth and how to harvest animals.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: Then we could get bigger and bigger populations, and the viruses went crazy.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And they went from animals to us.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: So measles went from cows to humans when humans learned to domesticate cows and started gathering in big cities.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: Yeah, but now that humans are able to communicate and travel globally, the viruses become more and more dangerous, transmissible.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: Thereby, if you look at Earth as an organism, thereby pushing humans to be more innovative, create Alpha-Fold 2 and 3 and 4 and 5, create better systems.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And eventually there's rockets that keep flying from Earth.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And eventually the virus is becoming super dangerous and threatening all of human civilization will force it to become a multi-planetary species, and its organism starts expanding.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: So I think it's a feature, not a bug. I don't know.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: Well, I think that we have our early... probably the most of the... we're studying viruses since 1900, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: Most of that time was because of diseases they caused.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: The first viruses discovered, yellow fever, virus, smallpox, polio virus, influenza virus, those were all because people got sick and they said,

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: oh, look, this is a virus that's associated with it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And so we got good at learning how to take care of these infections, making vaccines and so forth over the years.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And it's only in the last 20 years that we recognize that there are more viruses out there that are far more interesting, perhaps.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: But we've learned how to deal with the bad ones for sure.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: So we talked about what is a virus. We talked about some of the most dangerous and deadly viruses.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: Can we zoom in and talk about COVID-19 virus?

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: Sure.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: I don't know what your preferred name is, but...

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: Well, the virus is SARS-CoV-2, which is hard, it's long, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And then COVID-19 is the disease. So you could say the virus of COVID-19, that's fine.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: The virus of COVID-19. But for the purpose of this conversation, we'll every once in a while just say COVID.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: It's fine. No problem.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: What is this virus from? I don't know how many ways we can talk about it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: I think from a basic structural, like the variant structure, biological structure perspective, what is it? What are its variants?

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: Can you describe the basics, the important characteristics of the virus?

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: So viruses are classified by humans just to make it easier to keep track of them, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: So this is a coronavirus, which is because when they were first discovered, I think the first ones were animal coronaviruses.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: They looked at them in the electron microscope and it looked like the solar corona. And that's all there is to it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And I have to say that early in the outbreak, the place with the highest seropositivity in the US for a while, 68%, was a working class neighborhood in New York City called Corona.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: Can you beat that, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: That's crazy.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: So coronaviruses, they have membranes, right? We talked about membranes. They have spike proteins in the membrane so they can attach to cells.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And inside, they have RNA. And they are the viruses with the longest RNA that we know of. None other comes close.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: For some reason, they're able to maintain 30,000. So SARS-CoV-2 RNA is 30,000 bases of RNA. And some of the other coronas are even longer, 40,000.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: So this is a, coronas are family viruses that included the one you mentioned before, version one.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: So SARS-CoV-1, yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: CoV-1 and I guess other ones as well.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: So the first, we first learned of them in animals. A lot of animals, pigs and cows and horses have coronaviruses.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And then in the 60s, we discovered a couple of human coronaviruses that just cause colds, very mild colds that you wouldn't even think twice about, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And then suddenly in 2003, there's this outbreak of severe respiratory disease in China.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And it started in November and they didn't tell the world until February.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And that was really bad because it was already spreading by the time they told people about it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: But this went to 29 different countries. Only 8,000 people were infected and then it stopped.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And that was the first time we saw an epidemic coronavirus. And what they did afterwards is they said, OK, it looks like it came from the meat markets.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: They have live meat markets in Guangzhou in the south of China where you can go and pick out an animal and the guy will slaughter it for you and give it to you.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And then, of course, there's blood everywhere. And that's how they got infected.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And they figured out that there's this animal called a palm civet that was the source of virus.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: The palm civets are shipped in from the countryside and the palm civets somehow in the countryside got it from a bat.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: So they went looking in caves in the countryside and they found in one cave all the viruses that could make up SARS-1.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And that was 2012. I would say it took about five, eight years after that outbreak.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: So that was the first hint that bats have coronaviruses that can infect people and cause problems. Right.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And after that, we should have been ready. So didn't they already start developing vaccines?

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: Yes. So some people started making vaccines. They tested them in mice, but they never got into people.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And some people started working on antiviral drugs. Nothing ever came of them because, you know, industry, there's no there's no disease.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: It's gone. Why should we make vaccines and drugs? And NIH in the US, you submit a grant and they say, it's too risky.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: There's no none of this virus around. So people were really short sighted because I always say we could have had antivirals for this.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: Absolutely. Yeah. For sure. No question. In fact, one the one antiviral that's in phase three, it's called Molnupiravir.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: It's the only one that you can take orally. It's a pill. It looks really good.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: That was developed five years ago, but never taken into humans. It could have been ready.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: So we dropped the ball and then the next decade, 2012 MERS coronavirus comes comes up in the Arabian Peninsula.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: This comes from camels and infects people, but probably the camels got it from bats originally some time ago.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: But that never transmits from person to person. Very rarely. Every new little outbreak is a new infection from a camel.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: So that was 2012. And now here we are. 2019, the new outbreak of respiratory disease in China.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And this one really goes all over the world where SARS-1 could not. It's a coronavirus.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: You know, it's different enough from SARS-1 that it has very different properties. But it still has a membrane, still has a very long RNA in the middle.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And then it still has the spike proteins. That's right. What are the things that are what are the little unique things that make it that much more effective?

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: They make it cause a pandemic of millions of people as opposed to SARS-1.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: Well, the genome is 20 percent different from SARS-1, say.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And in those bases, there's some things that make it different from SARS-1. It binds the same receptor, ACE2, on the cell surface.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: That's remarkable. It has a lot of the same proteins. They look similar.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: Like if you look at the structure of the spikes, they look similar.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: But there's enough amino acid differences to make the biological. And what it is, we don't know because how do you figure that out?

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: You need to study animals because you can't infect people. And the animal models aren't great.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: So the way you figure that out is you figure out how those differences, what functional, like how the difference in the amino acids lead to functional difference of the virus.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: That's right. How it attaches, how it breaks the cell wall. Exactly. And how the hell do you figure that out?

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: Like, I guess there's models of interaction.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: First, you need an animal of some kind to infect. You can use mice. People have used ferrets, guinea pigs, non-human primates, all of the above.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: Non-human primates are very expensive, so not many people do that. And then you can put the virus in the respiratory tract.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: But in fact, none of them get sick like people do.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: Many people with COVID get a mild disease, but 20% get a very severe, longer lasting disease and they can die from it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: No animal does that yet. So we have no insight into what's controlling that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: But if you just want to look at the very first part of infection and the shedding and the transmission, you can do it in any one of several animal models.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: Ferrets are really good for transmission. They tend to have nasal structures like humans and you can put them in cages next to each other and they'll transmit the virus really nicely.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: So you can study that. But the other thing that's important that we should mention is how do you manipulate these viruses?

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: So these are RNA viruses. You can't manipulate RNA. We don't know how to do it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: DNA, because of the recombinant DNA revolution that occurred in the 70s, we can change DNA any way we want.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: We can change the single base. We can cut out bases. We can put other things in really easily.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And if I may give it a personal aspect, when I went to MIT as a postdoc in 1979, David Baltimore said,

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: Here's what I want you to do. The moratorium on recombinant DNA experiments on viruses has just been lifted.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: I want you to make a DNA copy of polio and see if you put that in a cell whether it will start an infection.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: It's okay. So I made a DNA copy of polio virus. It's only 7,500 bases. It's much smaller than corona.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And I took that DNA and I put it in a piece of DNA from a bacteria called a plasmid.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And you can grow plasmids in many, many bacteria, make lots of them and purify the DNA really easily.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And I took that DNA and I sequenced it because we didn't know the genome sequence of polio at the time.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And that took me a year, by the way, because the techniques we had were really archaic.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And nowadays you could do it in 15 minutes, right? It's amazing. And I took the DNA, I put it into cells and out came polio.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: So that's the start. Now, since then, everybody has taken that technique and used it for their virus.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: You can now do it with SARS-CoV-2. You make a DNA copy of any RNA virus.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: You can modify it and you put it back into cells and you'll get your modified virus out.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: So that's an important part of understanding the properties of the virus, let's say in an animal. By changing the virus, you're changing a DNA copy.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: You're making the virus then and putting it into the animal.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: Can you clarify? So even in the RNA virus, you can take and turn it into DNA?

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: Yes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And then that allows you to modify it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: Yes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: What's that mapping? No, no, no. What's the process of going from RNA to DNA?

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: Reverse transcription.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: That's reverse transcription. So you actually go through the process of reverse transcription to do this.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: Yes. Remember David Baltimore and Howard Tien have discovered this enzyme in the 70s. They got the Nobel Prize for that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And when I went to David's lab at MIT, he had the enzyme in the freezer. He said, here, take this and make a DNA copy of polio.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: Yeah, I didn't make the connection that you can use that kind of thing for an RNA virus and then modify it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: See, any DNA virus already exists as DNA, so you can modify it. But for RNA viruses, it was difficult.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And so then from that point on, for influenza, every other RNA virus and coronaviruses, people made DNA copies.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And that's what they use to modify and ask questions about what things are doing. What's this gene doing? What if we take it out? What happens?

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: Can you do the same thing with COVID? Take the RNA and then...

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: Of course. And in fact, in January 2020, as soon as the genome sequence was released from China, the labs all over were synthesizing this 30,000 base DNA and getting virus.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: What can you figure out without infecting anything? Just turning into, with reverse transcription, turning into DNA, modifying stuff, and then putting it into a cell. What can you figure out from that?

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: Well, you could, let's say you can cut out a gene. You see some genes in the sequence. I don't know what these genes do. Let's cut them out.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And then you could cut them out of the DNA. You put the DNA in cells and maybe you get virus out and you go, oh, clearly that gene's not needed for the virus to reproduce, at least in cells, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: Or maybe you take the gene out and you never get any virus. So it's lethal.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: Is there a nice systematic way of doing this? Do people kind of automate it?

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: Absolutely. And we, I mean, the problem with SARS, the COVID virus is it's 30,000 bases.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: It's long.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: There's a lot of stuff there. And what makes it more difficult is that you have to, it's been classified as a BSL3 agent, biosafety level three.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And so not everyone has a lab that's capable of doing that. So it limits the number of people who can do experiments.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: You know, some we were lucky to have a few in New York City, but not every place has them.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: So you cannot work with a virus just out on the bench like we do with many other viruses.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: You have to wear a suit and have to have special procedures and containment and so forth. So it makes it difficult to do basic experiments on the virus.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: But when it's a pandemic, there's a lot of money. There's a lot of incentive to work on it harder.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And also you don't need to work on the virus. You can take bits of it and work. You could say just the spike, right? And say, can we make a vaccine with just a spike?

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: That doesn't require BSL3. So yes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: So like building a vaccine requires you to figure out how or antiviral drugs, how to attack various structural parts of the virus and the functional parts of the virus.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: Right. You have to decide on a target.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: Yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: I'm going to make an antiviral. What am I going to target in the virus?

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And there are a few things that make more sense than others.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: Usually we like to target enzymes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: I don't know if you remember any your biochemistry, but you know, enzymes are catalytic.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: You don't need a lot of them to do a lot of things.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: So they're typically in low concentrations in a virus infected cell.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: So it's easier to inhibit them with a drug.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And the coronas have a couple of enzymes that we can target.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: So you have to figure that out ahead of time and decide what to go after.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And then you can look for drugs that inhibit what you're interested in. It's not that hard to do.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: There's just something beautiful about biology, about the mechanisms of biology.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And I kind of regret falling in love with computer science so much that I left that biology textbook on the show and left it behind.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: But hopefully we'll return to it now because I think one of the things you learn, even in computer science,

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: that studying biology and certainly neurobiology, you get inspired.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: Here's a mechanism of incredible complexity that works really well, is very robust, is very effective, efficient.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: It inspires you to come up with techniques that you can engineer in the machine.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: That's what drives the field forward when people improvise and come up with new technologies that really make a difference.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: We have a bunch of those now.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: What's the difference between the coronavirus family and the other popular family, influenza virus family?

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: I mean, because you mentioned we should have done a lot more in terms of vaccine development, that kind of thing for coronaviruses.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: But if I were back then, from my understanding, the thing we should all be afraid of is influenza,

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: like some strong variants coming out from that family, that seems like the one that will destroy human civilization or hurt us really badly.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: I don't know if you agree with this sense, but maybe you can also just clarify what to use is the difference between the families.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: So it's an interesting difference. They both have membranes, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: So then they have spike proteins embedded in them, and they're different spikes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: In fact, for influenza, there are two main ones. They're called the HA and the NA.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: But what's inside is RNA, but it's very different RNA.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And here we have to explain that. So viruses with RNA can have three different kinds of RNA.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: They can have what we call plus RNA. They can have minus RNA, or they could have plus minus, actually two strands hybridized together.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: The plus RNA simply means that if you put that plus RNA in a cell, your cell has ribosomes in it that make the proteins that you need.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: The ribosomes will immediately latch on to the plus RNA and begin to make proteins.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: A minus RNA is not the right strand to make proteins, so it has to be copied first. And then the plus minus is both together.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: So the SARS coronaviruses, all the coronaviruses have plus RNA. So as soon as that RNA gets in the cell, boom, it starts an infectious cycle.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: Same thing with poliovirus, by the way, which I worked on. Influenza viruses are negative stranded.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: So they cannot be translated when they get in the cell. So that's tough for the virus because the cell actually cannot make plus RNA from minus RNA.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: It doesn't have the enzyme to do it. So the virus has to carry it in inside the virus particle.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And then when the minus RNA is in the cell, the virus enzyme makes plus RNAs and those get translated. It's a big difference.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And then in the influenza viruses, not only is it minus RNA, but it's in pieces. It's in eight pieces.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: We call that segmented, whereas the corona is in one long piece of RNA.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: So what is that? Is it they're like floating separately?

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: Yeah. So the genes are on separate pieces. They're all packaged inside that virus particle of influenza virus, but they're in pieces.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And why that's important is because if two different influenza viruses infect the same cell, the pieces as they reproduce can mix and out can come a virus with a new assortment of pieces.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And that allows influenza virus to undergo extremely high frequency evolution. That's why we get pandemics.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And we have a new flu pandemics is because somewhere in some animal, two viruses have reassorted and made a new virus that we hadn't seen before.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: So you're talking about kind of biological characteristics, but what am I incorrect in my intuition that are from the things I've heard that the influence of a family of viruses is more dangerous?

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: Like what makes it more dangerous to humans?

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: Well, it depends on the there are many flavors or vintages of influenza virus. Some are dangerous and some are not.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: Right. It depends on which one. Some like the 1918 apparently was was very lethal, killed a lot of people.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: But more contemporary viruses. We had a pandemic in 2009 of influenza.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: That wasn't such a lethal virus. We don't know exactly why, but it didn't kill that many people. It transmitted pretty well. Is that the bird flu one?

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: They're all they're all deriving. That one was called swine influenza. Swine. It seemed to have started in a pig, but it had bird.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: It had RNAs from bird influenza viruses. These viruses are all reassortants of different viruses from pigs and birds and humans.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: But influenza can cause pneumonia and can kill you as does SARS-CoV-2. So it depends on the virus.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: So there is another influenza virus that's currently circulating. So right now we have the 2009 pandemic virus that's still around.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And then the 1968 pandemic virus, which was the one before 2009, that one is still around too. And that's more lethal.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And depending on the season, some seasons the 2009 virus predominates, some seasons the 1968. And when the 68 is around, you get more lethality.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: So we're living with an influenza family. We haven't exterminated them. Right. We never will never exterminate them. Why?

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: Well, because every shore bird in the world is infected with them, you know, gulls and terns and ducks and all sorts of things.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: But why can't we develop strong vaccines that defend against?

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: Oh, we could do that. Sure. But that would not eliminate them from humans. Even if you had the best vaccine, you would never get rid of it in people because there would always be someone who's not vaccinated or in which the vaccine didn't work.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: You know, no vaccine is 100 percent. Right. So you just contradict yourself. You had the, you said the perfect vaccine.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: So imperfect, but then you said, like, even if you had the perfect, yeah, some people wouldn't get vaccinated.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: But I understand what you mean. So I actually was asking, how difficult is it to make vaccines like that for it seems like it's very difficult to do that for the influenza virus.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: So it's really easy to make an old school vaccine.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: So the way the first influenza vaccines were made was actually Jonas Salk worked on them in the 40s.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: and some mucus which has virus and parts of virus,

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: and then you amplify it.

body.input: And you can specify what part of the viral RNA

body.input: you wanna amplify, and then a machine will detect it,

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: and it can be done in 15 minutes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: But you're detecting pieces of RNA, not infectious virus.

body.input: And a common mistake that many people who should know better,

body.input: It's a diagnostic of whether you have bits of RNA in you.

body.input: And it probably means you're infected,

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: but you can't use it to shed light on what's going on.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And I'll tell you why in a bit,

body.input: but first we have to explain some other things.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: So until you get to about a million copies of RNA,

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: so you can measure the copy number in this test,

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: this PCR test.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: It's a number called CT or cycle threshold.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: The test, the way the machine works,

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: it goes through cycles.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: In every cycle it amplifies what you put in.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And the more cycles you need to see something,

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: that means there's not a lot of RNA there.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: So if you do a test and you have a cycle threshold of 35,

body.input: you have a ton of RNA,

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: and it only took 10 cycles to detect it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And you can extrapolate from that number,

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: the number of copies you have per sample, say per swab.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And if you don't have a million, you're not infectious.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: You're not gonna infect anyone.

body.input: what PCR result you had, they would quarantine you.

body.input: And that was wrong because you're not shedding.

body.input: You don't need to be quarantined,

body.input: but wasn't thought through properly, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: And that's where you had like 14 days or something like that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Vincent Racaniello: Viruses and Vaccines | Lex Fridman Podcast #216

body.input: 14 days, which is now we know is too long
