metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: physics and I decided to go to Princeton and I started working with Edward Witten as my

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: thesis advisor. At that time, I was trying to put physics in rigorous mathematical theory.

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: I took quantum field theory, I tried to make rigorous out of it and so on. And no matter how

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: hard I was trying, I was not being able to do that. And I was falling behind from my classes. I was

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: not learning much physics and I was not making it rigorous. And to me, it was this dichotomy

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: between math and physics. What am I doing? I like math, but this is not exactly this.

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: There comes Edward Witten as my advisor and I see him in action.

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: Thinking about math and physics, he was amazing in math. He knew all about the math. It was no

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: problem with him, but he thought about physics in a way which did not find this tension between the

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: two. It was much more harmonious. For him, he would draw the Feynman diagrams, but he wouldn't

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: view it as a formalism. He was viewed, oh yeah, the particle goes over there and this is what's

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: going on. And I said, wait, you're thinking really as this particle, this is really electron going

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: there. Yeah, yeah, it's not the form of perturbation. No, no, no. You just feel like the

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: electron, you're moving with this guy and do that and so on. And you're thinking invariantly about

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: physics or the way he thought about relativity. I was thinking about this momentum. He was thinking

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: invariantly about physics, just like the way you think about invariant concepts in relativity,

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: which don't depend on the frame of reference. He was thinking about the physics in invariant ways,

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: the way that gives you a bigger perspective. So this gradually helped me appreciate that

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: interconnections between ideas and physics replaces mathematical rigor. The different facets

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: reinforce each other. They say, oh, I cannot rigorously define what I mean by this, but this

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: thing connects with this other physics I've seen and this other thing. And they together form an

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: elegant story. And that's replaced for me what I believed as a solidness, which I found in math

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: as a rigor, solid. I found that replaced the rigor and solidness in physics. So I found, okay,

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: that's the way you can hang on to. It is not wishy washy. It's not like somebody is just not

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: being able to prove it, just making up a story. It was more than that. And it was no tension with

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: mathematics. In fact, mathematics was helping it. Like friends, they were helping it. And

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: so it's much more harmonious and gives insights to physics. So that's, I think, one of the main

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: things I learned from interactions with Whitten. And I think that now perhaps I have taken that to

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: far extreme. Maybe he wouldn't go this far as I have. Namely, I use physics to define new

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: mathematics in a way which would be far less rigorous than a physicist might necessarily

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: believe because I take the physical intuition, perhaps literally in many ways that could teach

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: us a lot. So now I've gained so much confidence in physical intuition that I make bold statements

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: that sometimes takes math for instance off guard. So for an example of it is mirror symmetry.

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: So we were studying these compact fiational string geometry. This is after my PhD now.

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: By the time I've come to Harvard, we're studying these aspects of string compactification on these

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: complicated manifolds, six dimensional spaces called Kalab Yau manifolds, very complicated.

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: And I noticed with a couple other colleagues that there was a symmetry in physics suggested

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: between different Kalab Yau's. It suggested that you couldn't actually compute the Euler

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: characteristic of a Kalab Yau. Euler characteristic is counting the number of points minus the number

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: of edges plus the number of faces minus. So you can count the alternating sequence of properties

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: of a space, which is a topological property of a space. So Euler characteristic of the Kalab Yau

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: was a property of the space. And so we noticed that from the physics formalism, if string moves

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: in a Kalab Yau, you cannot distinguish, we cannot compute the Euler characteristic. You can only

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: compute the absolute value of it. Now this bothered us because how could you not compute the actual

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: sign unless the both sides were the same. So I conjectured maybe for every Kalab Yau with the

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: Euler characteristic positive, there's one with negative. I told this to my colleague, Yau, whose

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: namesake is Kalab Yau, that I'm making this conjecture. Is it possible that for every Kalab Yau

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: there's one with the opposite Euler characteristic? Sounds not reasonable. I said, why? He said, well,

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: we know more Kalab Yau's with negative Euler characteristic than positive.

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: I said, but physics says we cannot distinguish them. At least I don't see how. So we conjectured

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: that for every Kalab Yau with one sign, there's the other one, despite the mathematical evidence,

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: despite the mathematical evidence, despite the expert telling us it's not the right idea.

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: A few years later, this symmetry, mirror symmetry between the sign with the opposite sign was later

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: confirmed by mathematicians. So this is actually the opposite view. That is physics is so sure about

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: it that you're going against the mathematical wisdom telling them they better look for it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: So taking the the physical intuition literally and then having that drive the mathematics.

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: Exactly. And by now we are so confident about many such examples that has affected modern

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: mathematics in ways like this, that we are much more confident about our understanding of what

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: string theory is. These are other aspects, other aspects of why we feel string theory is crazy,

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: doing these kind of things. I've been hearing you talk quite a bit about string theory,

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: the quantum theory, landscape and the swamp land. What the heck are those two concepts?

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: Okay. Very good question. So let's go back to what I was describing about Feynman.

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: Yes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: Feynman was trying to do these diagrams for graviton and electrons and all that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: He found that he's getting infinities he cannot resolve. Okay. The natural conclusion is that

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: field theories and gravity and quantum theory don't go together and he cannot have it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: In other words, field theories and gravity are inconsistent with quantum mechanics period.

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: String theory came up with examples, but didn't address the question more broadly that

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: is it true that every field theory can be coupled to gravity in a quantum mechanical way?

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: It turns out that Feynman was essentially right. Almost all particle physics theories,

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: no matter what you add to it, when you put gravity in it, doesn't work. Only rare exceptions work.

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: So string theory are those rare exceptions. So therefore, the general principle that Feynman

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: found was correct. Quantum field theory and gravity and quantum mechanics don't go together,

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: except for Jules exceptional cases. There are exceptional cases.

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: Okay. The total vastness of quantum field theories that are there, we call the set of quantum field

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: theories, possible things. Which ones can be consistently coupled to gravity? We call that

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: subspace the landscape. The rest of them, we call the swampland. It doesn't mean they are bad

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: quantum field theories. They're perfectly fine. But when you couple them to gravity, they don't

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: make sense, unfortunately. And it turns out that the ratio of them, the number of theories which

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: are consistent with gravity to the ones without, the ratio of the area of the landscape to the

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: swampland, in other words, is measure zero. So the swampland is infinitely large?

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: The swampland is infinitely large. So let me give you one example. Take a theory in four dimension

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: with matter, with maximum amount of supersymmetry. It turns out a theory in four dimension with

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: maximum amount of supersymmetry is characterized just with one thing, a group, what we call the

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: gauge group. Once you pick a group, you have to find the theory. Okay. So does every group make

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: sense? Yeah. As far as quantum field theory, every group makes sense. There are infinitely many

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: groups. There are infinitely many quantum field theories. But it turns out there are only finite

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: number of them which are consistent with gravity out of that same list. So you can take any group,

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: but only find number of them. The ones who's what we call the rank of the group, the ones whose rank

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: is less than 23. Anyone bigger than rank 23 belongs to the swampland. There are infinitely

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: many of them. There are beautiful field theories, but not when you include gravity. So then this

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: becomes a hopeful thing. So in other words, in our universe, we have gravity. Therefore, we are part

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: of that dual subset. Now, is this dual subset small or large? It turns out that subset is humongous,

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: but we believe still finite. The set of possibilities is infinite, but the set of

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: consistent ones, I mean, the set of quantum features are infinite, but the consistent ones

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: are finite, but humongous. The fact that they're humongous is the problem we are facing in string

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: theory because we do not know which one of these possibilities is the universe we live in. If we

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: knew, we could make more specific predictions about our universe. We don't know. And that is one of

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: the challenges with string theory. Which point on the landscape, which corner of this landscape

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: do we live in? We don't know. So what do we do? Well, there are principles that are beginning to

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: emerge. So I will give you one example of it. You look at the patterns of what you're getting

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: in terms of these good ones, the ones which are in the landscape compared to the ones which are not.

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: You find certain patterns. I'll give you one pattern. You find in all the ones that you get

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: from string theory, gravitational force is always there, but it's always, always the weakest force.

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: However, you could easily imagine field theories for which gravity is not the weakest force. For

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: example, take our universe. If you increase the mass of electron by a huge factor,

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: the gravitational attraction of the electrons will be bigger than the electric repulsion between two

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: electrons, and the gravity will be stronger. That's all. It happens that it's not the case

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: in our universe because electron is very tiny in mass compared to that. Just like our universe,

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: gravity is the weakest force we find in all these other ones, which are part of the good ones,

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: the gravity is the weakest force. This is called the weak gravity conjecture. We conjecture that

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: all the points in the landscape have this property, our universe being just an example of it. So there

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: are these qualitative features that we are beginning to see, but how do we argue for this?

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: Just by looking patterns? Just by looking string theory as this? No, that's not enough.

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: We need more better reasoning, and it turns out there is. The reasoning for this turns out to be

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: studying black holes. Ideas of black holes turn out to put certain restrictions of what a good

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: quantum filter should be. It turns out using black hole, the fact that the black holes evaporate

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: gives you a way to check the relation between the mass and the charge of elementary particle,

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: because what you can do, you can take a charged particle and throw it into a charged black hole

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: and wait it to evaporate. By looking at the properties of evaporation, you find that if it

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: cannot evaporate particles whose mass is less than their charge, then it will never evaporate. You

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: will be stuck. So the possibility of a black hole evaporation forces you to have particles whose

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: mass is sufficiently small so that the gravity is weaker. So you connect this fact to the other

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: fact. So we begin to find different facts that reinforce each other. So different parts of the

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: physics reinforce each other, and once they all kind of come together, you believe that you're

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: getting the principle correct. So weak gravity conjecture is one of the principles we believe in

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: as a necessity of these conditions. So these are the predictions Trinity are making. Is that enough?

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: Well, it's qualitative. It's a semi-quantity. It's just the mass of the electron should be less than

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: some number. But that number, if I call that number one, the mass of the electron turns out to be 10

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: to the minus 20 actually. So it's much less than one. It's not one. But on the other hand,

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: there's a similar reasoning for a big black hole in our universe. And if that evaporation should

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: take place, gives you another restriction, tells you the mass of the electron is bigger than 10 to

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: the, now in this case, bigger than something. It shows bigger than 10 to the minus 30 in the

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: Planck unit. So you find, aha, the mass of the electron should be less than one, but bigger than

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: the mass of the electron should be less than one, but bigger than 10 to the minus 30. In our universe,

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: the mass of the electrons tends to minus 20. Okay. Now this kind of you could call post-diction,

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: but I would say it follows from principles that we now understand from string theory,

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: first principle. So we are beginning to make these kinds of predictions, which are very much

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: connected to aspects of particle physics that we didn't think are related to gravity. We thought,

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: just take any electron mass you want. What's the problem? It has a problem with gravity.

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: And so that conjecture has also a happy consequence that it explains that our universe,

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: like why the heck is gravity so weak as a force? And that's not only an accident, but almost a

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: necessity if these forces are to coexist effectively. Exactly. So that's the reinforcement

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: of what we know in our universe, but we are finding that as a general principle. So we want

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: to know what aspects of our universe is forced on us, like the weak gravity conjecture and other

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: aspects. How much of them do we understand? Can we have particles lighter than neutrinos? Or maybe

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: that's not possible. You see the neutrino mass, it turns out to be related to dark energy in a

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: mysterious way. Naively, there's no relation between dark energy and the mass of a particle.

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: We have found arguments from within the Swamp Land kind of ideas, why it has to be related.

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: And so they're beginning to be these connections between consistency of quantum gravity and

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: aspects of our universe gradually being sharpened. But we are still far from a precise quantitative

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: prediction, like we have to have such and such, but that's the hope, that we are going in that

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: followed their own interests. And I think that's the advice I would give to any young person,

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: follow your own interests and let it, that take you wherever it takes you. And this I did

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: verified even, let alone apply to the daily technology in our lifetime. I'm lucky I'm doing

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: that. And I feel that if people follow their interests, they will find the niche that they're

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: good at. And this coincidence of hopefully their interests and abilities are kind of aligned,

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: or this doesn't do that, and my parents expect that, or what about this? And I think ultimately

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: pave a path, that will find a way to make money, especially in this society, in the capitalistic

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: do much about. And I think it's something that it doesn't drive my everyday action. It is natural

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: to expect that it's somewhat like the time reversal situation. So we believe that we have

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: this approximate symmetry in nature, time reversal. Going forward, we die. Going backwards, we get

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: born. So what was it to get born? It wasn't such a good or bad thing. I have no feeling of it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: So who knows what the death will feel like, the moment of death or whatnot. So I don't know.

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: It is not known. But in what form do we exist before or after? Again, it's something that

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: it's partly philosophical maybe. I like how you draw comfort from symmetry. It does seem

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: that there is something asymmetric here, a breaking of symmetry, because there's something

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: stuff together. Yes, I think that's true. But actually, I have a different perspective on that

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: a little bit. Namely, suppose I told you you're immortal. I think your life will be totally

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: boring after that, because I think part of the reason we have enjoyment in life is the

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: finiteness of it. And so I think mortality might be a blessing and immortality may not.

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: So I think that we value things because we have that finite life. We appreciate things. We want

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: to do this. We want to do that. We have motivation. If I told you, you have infinite life. Oh, I don't

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: finiteness of these resources. So I think it is a blessing in disguise. I don't regret it that we

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: have a more finite life. And I think that the process of being part of this thing, the reality,

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: to me, part of what attracts me to science is to connect to that immortality,

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: kind of, namely the loss, the reality beyond us. To me, I'm resigned to the fact that not only me,

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: everybody is going to die. So this gives a little bit of a consolation. None of us are going to be

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: around. So therefore, okay. And none of the few before me are around. So therefore, yeah, okay.

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: This is something everybody goes through. So taking that minuscule version of, okay, how tiny we are

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: and how short time it is and so on, to connect to the deeper truth beyond us, the reality beyond us,

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: is what sense of quote unquote immortality I would get. Namely, I at least I can hang on to this

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: know it's going to change and it's going to be improved. But having a little bit deeper insight

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: than just the naive thing around us, little earth here and little galaxy and so on, makes me feel a

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

metadata.title: Podcast: Cumrun Vafa: String Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #204

body.input: Hello World is the first thing that you do in every computer programming language and every computer.

body.input: But not having any interaction with the cultures of Unix or any other standardized things,

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: Can I ask you a programming advice? I was always told in the beginning that you're not allowed to use Go to statements.

body.input: That's really bad programming. Is this correct or not? Jumping around code.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: That seems so convenient, but it's supposed to be bad programming.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: Well, so certainly back in the day in basic programming languages, you didn't have proper loops.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: You didn't have four whiles and repeats.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: That was the land of Pascal for people that kind of generally had access to it back then.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: So you had no choice but to use Go tos.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: And as you made what were big programs back then, which were a thousand line basic program,

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: is a really big program. They did tend to sort of degenerate into madness.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: So you would wind up fixing things in one place, add a little patch.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: And there's reasons why structured programming generally helps understanding.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: the more of these like hacks you're going to see because the set of features available to you in low level programming languages is not is limited.

body.input: So print John Carmack, when is the first time, if we could talk about love, that you fell in love with programming?

body.input: You said like this, this is really something special.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: It really was something that was one of those love at first sight things where just really from the time that I understood what a computer was,

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: even I mean, I remember looking through old encyclopedias at the black and white photos of the IBM mainframes with the reel to reel tape decks.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: And for people nowadays, it can be a little hard to understand what the world was like then from information gathering,

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: where I would go to the libraries and there would be a couple books on the shelf about computers and they would be very out of date.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: Even at that point, just not a lot of information, but I would grab everything that I could find and devour everything.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: It felt like this magical thing to me, this idea that the computer would just do exactly what you told it to.

body.input: But it wasn't going to backtalk you. It wasn't going to have a different point of view.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: It was going to carry out what you told it to do.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: And if you had the right commands, you could make it do these pretty magical things.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: And so what kind of programs did you write at first?

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: Beyond the Print, John Carmack.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: So I can remember as going through the learning process where you find at the start, you're just learning how to do the most basic possible things.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: And I can remember stuff like a Superman comic that Radio Shack commissioned to have.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: It's like Superman had lost some of his super brain and kids had to use Radio Shack TRS-80 computers to do calculations for it to help him kind of complete his heroics.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: And I'd find little things like that and then get a few basic books to be able to kind of work my way up.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: And again, it was so precious back then. I had a couple books that would teach me important things about it.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: I had one book that I could start to learn a little bit of assembly language from.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: And I'd have a few books on basic and some things that I could get from the libraries.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: But my goals in the early days was almost always making games of various kinds.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: I loved the arcade games and the early Atari 2600 games.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: And being able to do some of those things myself on the computers was very much what I aspired to.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: And it was a whole journey where if you learn normal basic, you can't do any kind of an action game.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: You can write an adventure game. You can write things where you say, what do you do here?

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: Get sword, attack troll, that type of thing. And that can be done in the context of basic.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: But to do things that had moving graphics, there were only the most limited things you could possibly do.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: You could maybe do breakout or pong or that sort of thing in low resolution graphics.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: And in fact, one of my first sort of major technical hacks that I was kind of fond of was on the Apple II computers.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: They had a mode called low resolution graphics where, of course, all graphics were low resolution back then.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: But regular low resolution graphics, it was a grid of 40 by 40 pixels normally, but they could have 16 different colors.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: And I wanted to make a game kind of like the arcade game Vanguard, just a scrolling game.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: And I wanted to just kind of have it scroll vertically up. And I could move a little ship around.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: You could manage to do that in basic, but there's no way you could redraw the whole screen.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: And I remember at the time just coming up with what felt like a brainstorm to me where I knew enough

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: about the way the hardware was controlled, where the text screen and the low resolution graphics screen were basically the same thing.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: And all those computers could scroll their text screen reasonably. You could do a listing and it would scroll things up.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: And I figured out that I could kind of tweak just a couple things that I barely understood to put it into a graphics mode.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: And I could draw graphics and then I could just do a line feed at the very bottom of the screen.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: And then the system would scroll it all up using an assembly language routine that I didn't know how to write back then.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: So that was like this first great hack that sort of had analogs later on in my career for a lot of different things.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: So I found out that I could draw a screen, I could do a line feed at the bottom, it would scroll it up once.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: I could draw a couple more lines of stuff at the bottom. And that was my first way to kind of scroll the screen,

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: which was interesting in that that played a big part later on in the id software days as well.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: So do efficient drawing where you don't have to draw the whole screen,

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: but you draw from the bottom using the thing that was designed in the hardware for text output.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: Yeah. Where so much of, until recently, game design was limited by what you could actually get the computer to do.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: Where it's easy to say, like, OK, I want to scroll the screen. You just redraw the entire screen at a slight offset.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: And nowadays that works just fine. Computers are ludicrously fast.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: But up until a decade ago or so, there were all these things everybody wanted to do.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: But if they knew enough programming to be able to make it happen, it would happen too slow to be a good experience,

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: either just ridiculously slow or just slow enough that it wasn't fun to experience it like that.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: So so much of kind of the first couple decades of the programming work that I did was largely figuring out

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: how to do something that everybody knows how they want it to happen.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: It just has to happen two to ten times faster than sort of the straightforward way of doing things would make it happen.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: And it's different now because at this point, lots of things you can just do in the most naive possible way.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: And it still works out. You know, you don't have nearly the creative limitations or the incentives for optimizing on that level.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: And there's a lot of pros and cons to that. But I do generally, you know,

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: I'm not going to do the the angry old man shaking my fist at the clouds bit where back in my day programmers had to do real programming.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: You know, it's it's amazing that you can just kind of pick an idea and go do it right now.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: And you don't have to be some assembly language wizard or deep GPU arcaneist to be able to figure out how to make your wishes happen.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: Well, there's still see that's true. But let me put on my old man with a fist hat and say that probably the thing that will define the future

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: still requires you to operate at the limits of the current system.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: So we'll probably talk about this. But if you talk about building the metaverse and building a VR experience that's compelling,

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: it probably requires you to not to go to assembly or maybe not literally,

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: but sort of spiritually to go to the limits of what the system is capable of.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: And that really was why virtual reality was specifically interesting to me, where it had all the ties to you could say that even back in the early days,

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: I have some old magazine articles that's talking about doom as a virtual reality experience back when just seeing anything in 3D.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: So you could say that we've been trying to build those virtual experiences from the very beginning.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: And in the modern era of virtual reality, especially on the mobile side of things,

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: when it's standalone, you're basically using a cell phone chip to be able to produce these very immersive experiences.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: It does require work. It's not at the level of what an old school console game programmer would have operated at,

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: where you're looking at hardware registers and you're scheduling all the DNA accesses.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: But it is still definitely a different level than what a web developer or even a PC Steam game developer usually has to work at.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: And again, it's great. There's opportunities for people that want to operate at either end of that spectrum there and still provide a lot of value to the world.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: Let me ask you sort of a big question about preference.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: What would you say is the best programming language? Your favorite, but also the best you've seen throughout your career.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: You're considered by many to be the greatest programmer ever.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: I mean, it's so difficult to place that label on anyone. But if you put it on anyone, it's you.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: So let me ask you these kind of ridiculous questions of what's the best band of all time?

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: But in your case, what's the best programming language?

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: Everything has all the caveats about it. So what I use. So nowadays I do program a reasonable amount of Python for AIML sorts of work.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: I'm not a native Python programmer. It's something I came to very late in my career. I understand what it's good for.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: You don't dream in Python. I do not.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: And it has some of those things where there are some amazing stats.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: When you say if you just start, if you make a loop, you know, a triply nested loop and start doing operations in Python,

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: you can be thousands to potentially a million times slower than a proper GPU tensor operation.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: And these are staggering numbers. You know, you can be as much slower as we've almost gotten faster in our pace of progress and all this other miraculous stuff.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: So your intuitions about inefficiencies within the Python sort of.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: It keeps hitting me upside the face where it just it's gotten to the point now I understand it's like, OK, you just can't do a loop if you care about performance in Python.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: You have to figure out how you can reformat this into some big vector operation or something that's going to be done completely within a C++ library.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: But the other hand is it's it's amazingly convenient.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: And you just see stuff that people are able to cobble together by you just import a few different things and you can do stuff that nobody on Earth could do 10 years ago.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: And you can do it in a little cookbook thing that you copy paste it out of a website.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: So that is really great. When I'm sitting down to do what I consider kind of serious programming, it's still in C++.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: And it's really kind of a C flavored C++ at that where I'm not big into the modern template metaprogramming sorts of things.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: I see a lot of train wrecks coming from some of that over abstraction.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: I spent a few years really going kind of deep into the kind of the historical Lisp work and the Haskell and some of the functional programming sides of things.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: And there's. There is a lot of value there in the way you think about things.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: And I changed a lot of the way I write my C and C++ code based on what I learned about the value that comes out of not having this random mutable state that you kind of lose track of.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: Because something that many people don't really appreciate till they've been at it for a long time is that it's not the writing of the program.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: Initially, it's the whole lifespan of the program.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: And that's when it's not necessarily just how fast you wrote it or how fast it operates, but it's how can it bend and adapt as situations change?

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: And then the thing that I've really been learning in my time at Meta with the Oculus and VR work is it's also how well it hands off between the continuous kind of revolving door programmers taking over maintenance and different things and how you get people up to speed in different areas.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: And there's all these other different aspects of it.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: So C++ a good language for handover between engineers.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: Probably not the best.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: And there's some really interesting aspects to this where in some cases, languages that are not that are not generally thought well of for many reasons like C is derided pretty broadly that yes, obviously all of these security flaws that happen with the memory and unsafeness and buffer overruns and the things that you've got there.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: But there is this underappreciated aspect to the language is so simple.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: Anyone can go and if you know C, you can generally jump in someplace and not have to learn what paradigms they're using because there just aren't that many available.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: I think there's some really, really well written C code.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: I find it great that if I'm messing around with something in OpenBSD, say, I can be walking around in the kernel and I'm like, I understand everything that's going on here.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: It's not hard for me to figure out what I need to do to make whatever change that I need to.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: While you can have more significant languages like it's a downside of Lisp where I don't regret the time that I spent with Lisp.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: I think that it did help my thinking about programming in some ways.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: But the people that are the biggest defenders of Lisp are saying how malleable of a language it is that if you write a huge Lisp program, you've basically invented your own kind of language and structure because it's not the primitives of the language you're using very much.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: It's all of the things you've built on top of that.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: And then a language like Racket, kind of one of the more modern Lisp versions, it's essentially touted as a language for building other languages.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: And I understand the value of that for a tiny little project.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: But the idea of that for one of these long term supported by lots of people kind of horrifies me where all of those abstractions that you're like, OK, you can't touch this code till you educate yourself on all of these things that we've built on top of that.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: And it was interesting to see how when Google made Go, a lot of the criticisms of that are it's like, wow, this is not a state of the art language. This language is just so simple and almost crude.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: And you could see the programming language people just looking down at it.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: But it does seem to be quite popular as basically saying this is the good things about C. Everybody can just jump right in and use it.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: You don't need to restructure your brain to write good code in it.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: So I wish that I had more opportunity for doing some work in Go.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: Rust is the other modern language that everybody talks about that I'm not fit to pass judgment on.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: I've done a little bit beyond Hello World. I wrote some video decompression work in Rust just as an exercise.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: But that was a few years ago and I haven't really used it since.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: The best programming language is the one that works generally that you're currently using.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: Because that's another trap is in almost every case I've seen when people mixed languages on a project, that's a mistake.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: I would rather stay just in one language so that everybody can work across the entire thing.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: And we have like at Meta, we have a lot of projects that use kind of React framework.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: So you've got JavaScript here and then you have C++ for real work.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: And then you may have Java interfacing with some other part of the Android system.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: And those are all kind of horrible things. And that was one thing that I remember talking with Boz at Facebook about it.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: Where like, man, I wish we could have just said we're only hiring C++ programmers.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: And he just thought from the Facebook Meta perspective, well, we just wouldn't be able to find enough.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: With the thousands of programmers they've got there, it is not necessarily a dying breed.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: But you can sure find a lot more Java or JavaScript programmers.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: And I kind of mentioned that to Elon one time and he was kind of flabbergasted about that.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: It's like, well, you just you go out and you find those programmers and you don't hire the other programmers that don't do the languages that you want to use.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: But right now, I guess, yeah, they're using JavaScript on a bunch of the SpaceX work for the UI side of things.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: When you go find UI programmers, they're JavaScript programmers.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: I wonder if that's because there's a lot of JavaScript programmers, because I do think that great programmers are rare.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: That it's not, you know, if you just look at statistics of how many people are using different programming languages, that doesn't tell you the story of what the great programmers are using.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: And so you have to really look at what you were speaking to, which is the fundamentals of a language.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: What does it encourage? How does it encourage you to think? What kind of systems does it encourage you to build?

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: There is something about C++ that has elements of creativity, but forces you to be an adult about your programming.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: It expects you to be an adult. It does not force you to.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: And so it brings out people that are willing to be creative in terms of building large systems and coming up with interesting solutions,

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: but at the same time have the sort of the good software engineering practices that amend themselves to real world systems.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: Let me ask you about this other language, JavaScript.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: So if we, you know, aliens visit in thousands of years and humans are long gone, something tells me that most of the systems they find will be running JavaScript.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: I kind of think that if the simulat, if we're living in a simulation, it's written in JavaScript.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: You know, for the longest time, even still, JavaScript didn't get any respect.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: And yet it runs so much of the world and an increasing number of the world.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: Is it possible that all everything will be written in JavaScript one day?

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: So the engineering under JavaScript is really pretty phenomenal.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: The systems that make JavaScript run as fast as it does right now are kind of miracles of modern engineering in many ways.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: It does feel like it is not an optimal language for all the things that it's being used for or an optimal distribution system to build huge apps in something like this without type systems and so on.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: But I think for a lot of people, it does reasonably the necessary things.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: It's still a sea flavored language. It's still a braces and semicolon language.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: It's not hard for people to be trained in JavaScript and then understand the roots of where it came from.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: I think garbage collection is unequivocally a good thing for most programs to be written in.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: It's funny that I still just this morning I was on I was seeing a Twitter thread of a bunch of really senior game dev people arguing about the virtues and costs of garbage collection.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: You will run into some people that are top notch programmers that just say, no, this is literally not a good thing.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: Because it makes you lazy.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: Yes, that it makes you not think about things.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: And I do disagree.

metadata.title: Podcast: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309

body.input: I think that there is so much objective data on the vulnerabilities that have happened in C and C++ programs, sometimes written by the best programmers in the world.
