metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: And the other one is like an incredible Silicon Valley programmer that's

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: programmed in everything, C, C++, Python, Rust, Java, and knows the entire

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: history of programming languages.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: So you're going to have to speak to both.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: I imagine that boat in the middle of the ocean.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: I'm going to please the guy who knows how to fish first.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Yes, please.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: He seems like the most useful in the middle of the ocean.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: You got to make him happy.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: I'm sure he has a cell phone.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: So he's probably very suspicious about what goes on in that cell phone, but he

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: must have heard that inside a cell phone is a tiny computer and a programming

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: language is computer code that tells the computer what to do.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: It's a very low level language.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: It's zeros and ones, and then there's assembly and then, oh, yeah,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: we don't talk about these really low levels because those just confuse people.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: I mean, when we're talking about human language, we're not usually talking

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: about vocal tracts and how you position your tongue.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: I was talking yesterday about how when you have a Chinese person and they

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: speak English, this is a bit of a stereotype they often don't know.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: They can't seem to make the difference well between an L and an R.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: And I have a theory about that and I've never checked this with linguists

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: that it probably has to do with the fact that in Chinese there is not really a

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: difference and it could be that there are regional variations in how

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: native Chinese speakers pronounce that one sound that sounds like L to some

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: of them, like R to others.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: So it's both the sounds you produce with your mouth throughout the history of

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: your life and what you're used to listening to.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: I mean, every language has that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Russian has the Slavic languages have sounds like the letters, like Americans

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: or English speakers don't seem to know the sound.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: They seem uncomfortable with that sound.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: So, yes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Okay.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: So we're not talking about the sound of the tongue.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: So, yes, okay.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: So we're not going to the shapes of tongues and the sounds that the mouth can make.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: And similarly, we're not going into the ones and zeros or machine language.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: I would say a programming language is a list of instructions, like a cookbook

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: recipe that sort of tells you how to do a certain thing, like make a sandwich.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Well, acquire a loaf of bread, cut it in slices.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Take two slices, put mustard on one, put the jelly on the other or something.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Then add the meat, then add the cheese.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: I've heard that science teachers can actually do great stuff with recipes

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: like that and trying to interpret their students' instructions incorrectly

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: until the students are completely unambiguous about it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: With language, see, that's the difference between natural languages

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: and programming languages.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: I think ambiguity is a feature, not a bug in human spoken languages.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Like that's the dance of communication between humans.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Well, for lawyers, ambiguity certainly is a feature.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: For plenty of other cases, the ambiguity is not much of a feature,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: but we work around it, of course.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: What's more important is context.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: So with context, the precision of the statement becomes more and more concrete.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Right.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: But when you say, I love you to a person that matters a lot to you, the person

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: doesn't try to compile that statement and return an error saying, please define love.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: No, but I imagine that my wife and my son interpret it very differently.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Yes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Even though it's the same three words.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: But imprecisely still.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Oh, for sure.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Lawyers have a lot of follow up questions for you.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Nevertheless, the context is already different in that case.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Yes, fair enough.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: So that's a programming language is ability to unambiguously state a recipe.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Actually, let's go back.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Let's go to Pepe.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: You go through and Pepe, the style guy for Python code, some ideas.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Some ideas of what this language should look like, feel like, read like.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: And the big idea there is that code readability counts.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: What does that mean to you?

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: And how do we achieve it?

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: So this recipe should be readable.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: That's a thing between programmers.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Because on the one hand, we always explain the concept of programming

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: language as computers need instructions and computers are very dumb and they

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: need very precise instructions because they don't have much context.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: In fact, they have lots of context, but their context is very different.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: But what we've seen emerge during the development of software, starting

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: in the probably in the late forties, is that software is a very social activity.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: A software developer is not a mad scientist who sits alone in

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: his lab writing brilliant code.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Software is developed by teams of people.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Even the mad scientist sitting alone in his lab can type fast enough to produce

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: enough code so that by the time he's done with his coding, he still remembers

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: what the first few lines he wrote mean.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: So even the mad scientist coding alone in his lab would be sort of wise to adopt

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: conventions on how to format the instructions that he gives to the computer.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: So that the thing is there is a difference between a cookbook recipe and a computer program.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: The cookbook recipe, the author of the cookbook writes it once and then it's

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: printed in a hundred thousand copies.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: And then lots of people in their kitchens try to recreate that recipe, that

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: particular pie or dish from the recipe.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: And so there the goal of the cookbook author is to make it clear to the human

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: reader of the recipe, the human amateur chef in most cases.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: When you're writing a computer program, you have two audiences at once.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: It needs to tell the computer what to do, but it also is useful if that program

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: is readable by other programmers because computer software, unlike the typical

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: recipe for a cherry pie is so complex that you don't get all of it right at once.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: You end up with the activity of debugging.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: And you end up with the activity of, so debugging is trying to figure out why

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: your code doesn't run the way you thought it should run.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: That means broadly, it could be stupid little errors or it could be big logical errors.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: It could be anything spiritual.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: It could be anything from a typo to a wrong choice of algorithm to building

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: something that does what you tell it to do, but that's not useful.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: It seems to work really well 99% of the time, but does weird things

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: 1% of the time on some edge cases.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Well, that's pretty much all software nowadays.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: All good software, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Well, yeah, for, for bad software that 99 goes down a lot.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: So, but it's not just about the complexity of the program.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: It's like you said, it is a social endeavor.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: In that you're constantly improving that recipe for the cherry pie, but you're

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: sort of, you're in a group of people improving that recipe or the mad

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: scientist is improving the recipe that he created a year ago and making it better.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Or adding, adding something.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: He decides that he wants a, I don't know, he wants some decoration on his pie or icing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: So there's broad philosophical things and there's specific advice on style.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: So first of all, the thing that people first experience when they look at Python,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: there is a, it is very readable, but there's also like a spatial structure to it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Can you explain the indentation style of Python and what is the magic to it?

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Spaces are important for readability of any kind of text.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: If you take a cookbook recipe and you remove all the sort of, all the bullets

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: and other markup, and you just crunch all the text together, maybe you leave

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: the spaces between the words, but that's all you leave when you're in the kitchen

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: trying to figure out, Oh, what are the ingredients and what are the steps and

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: where does the writing come from?

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: What are the ingredients and what are the steps and where does this step end?

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: And the next step begin, you're going to have a hard time if it's, if it's just

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: one solid block of text.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: On the other hand, what, what a typical cookbook does, if the paper is not too

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: expensive, each recipe starts on its own page.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Maybe there's a picture next to it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: The list of ingredients comes first.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: There's a standard notation, there's shortcuts so that you don't have to sort

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: of write two sentences on how you have to cut the onion because there are only

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: three ways that people ever cut onions in a kitchen, small, medium and in

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: slices or something like that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Right.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: None of my examples make any sense to real cooks, of course, but.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: We're talking to programmers with the metaphor of cooking.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: I love it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: But there is a strictness to the spacing that Python defines.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: So there's some looser things, some stricter things, but the four spaces

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: for the, for the indentation is really interesting.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: It, it really, it really defines what the language looks and feels like.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Because indentation sort of taking a block of text and then having inside

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: that block of text, a smaller block of text that is indented further and

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: further away, as sort of a group.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: It's, it's, it's like you have a bulleted list in a complex business

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: document and inside some of the bullets are other bulleted lists.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: You will indent those too.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: If each bulleted list is indented several inches, then at two levels

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: deep, there's no, no space left on the page to put any of the words of the text.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: So you can't indent too far.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: You can't indent at all.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: You can tell whether something is a top level bullet or a second level

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: bullet or a third level bullet.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: So you have to have some compromise and based on ancient conventions and the

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: sort of the typical width of a computer screen in the eighties and all sorts

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: of things, sort of, we came up with sort of four spaces as a compromise.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: I mean, there are groups, there are large groups of people who code with two

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: spaces per indent level, for example, the Google style guide, all the Google

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Python code, and I think also all the Google C++ code is indented with only

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: two spaces per block.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: If you're not used to that, it's harder to at a glance understand the code

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: because the sort of the high level structure is determined by the indentation.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: On the other hand, there are other programming languages where the indentation

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: is eight spaces or a whole tap stop in sort of classic Unix.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: And to me, that looks weird because you sort of after three indent levels, you've

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: got no room left.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Well, there's some languages where the indentation is a recommendation.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: It's a stylistic one.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: The code compiles even without any indentation.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: And then Python really indentation is a fundamental part of the language.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Right.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: It doesn't have to be four spaces.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: So you can code Python with two spaces per block or four or six spaces or

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: 12, if you really want to go wild.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: But sort of everything that belongs to the same block needs to be indented the

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: same way in practice, in most other languages, people recommend doing that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Anyway, if you look at C or Rust or C++, all those languages, Java don't have a

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: requirement of indentation, but except in extreme cases, they're just as

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: anal about having their code properly indented.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: So any IDE that the syntax highlighting that works with Java or C++, they will

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: yell at you aggressively if you don't do proper indentation.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: They'd suggest the proper indentation for you.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Like in C you type a few words and then you type a curly brace, which is their

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: notion of sort of begin an indented block.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Then you hit return and then it automatically indents four or eight spaces,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: depending on your style preferences or how your editor is configured.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Was there a possible universe in which you considered having braces in Python?

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Absolutely.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: What was the 60, 40, 70, 30 in your head?

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: What was the trade off?

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: For a long time, I was actually convinced that the indentation was just better.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Without context, I would still claim that indentation is better.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: It reduces clutter.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: However, as I started to say earlier, context is almost everything.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: In the context of coding, most programmers are familiar with multiple

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: languages, even if they're only good at one or two.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Apart from Python and maybe Fortran, I don't know how that's written these days

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: anymore, but all the other languages, Java, Rust, C, C++, JavaScript, TypeScript,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Perl are all using curly braces to sort of indicate blocks.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: And so Python is the odd one out.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: So it's a radical idea.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Do you still, as a radical renegade revolutionary, do you still stand behind

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: this idea of indentation versus braces?

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: What can you dig into it a little bit more?

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Why you still stand behind this idea of indentation versus braces?

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Why you still stand behind indentation?

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Because context is not the whole story.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: History, in a sense, provides more context.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: So for Python, there's no chance that we can switch.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Python is using curly braces for something else, dictionaries mostly.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: We would get in trouble if we wanted to switch.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Just like you couldn't redefine C to use indentation, even if you agree that

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: indentation sort of in a greenfield environment would be better.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: You can't change that kind of thing in a language.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: It's hard enough to reach agreement over much more minor details.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Maybe, I mean, in the past in Python, we did have a big debate about

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: TEPs versus spaces and four spaces versus fewer or more.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: And we sort of came up with a recommended standard and sort of options

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: for people who want to be different.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: But yes, I guess the thought experiment I'd like you to consider is if you

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: could travel back through time when the compatibility is not an issue.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: And you started Python all over again.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Can you make the case for indentation still?

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Well, it frees up a pair of matched brackets of which there are never

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: enough in the world for other purposes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: It really makes the language slightly easier to grasp for people who don't

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: already know another programming language.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Because the sort of one of the things, and I mostly got this from my mentors

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: who taught me programming language design in the earlier eighties, when

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: you're teaching programming for the total newbie who has not coded before

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: in not in any other language, a whole bunch of concepts in programming are

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: very alien or sort of new and maybe very interesting, but also distracting

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: and confusing, and there are many different things you have to learn.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: You have to sort of in a typical 13 week programming course, you have to,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: if it's like really learning to program from scratch, you have to cover

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: algorithms, you have to cover data structures.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: You have to cover syntax, you have to cover variables, loops, functions,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: recursion, classes, expressions, operators.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: There are so many concepts.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: If you can spend a little less time having to worry about the syntax.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: The classic example was often, oh, the components of the code.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: The compiler complains every time I put a semi-column in the wrong place, or

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: I forget to put a semi-column.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Python doesn't have semi-columns in that sense.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: So you can't forget them.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: And you are also not sort of misled into putting them where they don't belong

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: because you don't learn about them in the first place.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: The flip side of that is forcing the strictness onto the beginning programmer.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: To teach them that programming values attention to details.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: You don't get to just write the way you write in English.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: There are many other details that they have to pay attention to.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: So I think they'll still get the message about paying attention to detail.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: The interesting design choice, I still program quite a bit in PHP and I'm

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: sure there's other languages like this, but the dollar sign before a variable.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: That was always an annoying thing for me.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: It didn't quite fit into my understanding of why this is good for a programming

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: language.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: I'm not sure if you ever thought about that one.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: That is a historical thing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: There is a whole lineage of programming languages.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: PHP is one.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Perl was one.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: The Unix shell is one of the oldest or all the different shells.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: The dollar was invented for that purpose because the very earliest shells had a

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: notion of scripting, but they did not have a notion of parameterizing the scripting.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: A script is just a few lines of text where each line of text is a command that is

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: read by a very primitive command processor that then sort of takes the first word on

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: the line as the name of a program and passes all the rest of the line as text

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: into the program for the program to figure out what to do with as arguments.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: And so by the time scripting was slightly more mature than the very first script,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: there was a convention that just like the first word on the line is the name of the

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: program, the following words could be names of files, input.text, output.html,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: things like that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: The next thing that happens is, oh, it would actually be really nice if we could have

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: variables and especially parameters for scripts.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Parameters are usually what starts this process.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: But now you have a problem because you can't just say the parameters are X, Y, and Z.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: And so now we call, say, let's say X is the input file and Y is the output file.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: And let's forget about Z for now.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: I have my program and I write program.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: X, Y. Well, that already has a meaning because that presumably means X itself is

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: the file.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: It's a file name.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: It's not a variable name.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: And so the inventors of things like the Unix shell and I'm sure job command

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: language at IBM before that had to use a lot of different tools.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Had to use something that made it clear to the script processor.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Here is an X that is not actually the name of a file, which you just pass through to

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: the program you're running.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Here is an X that is the name of a variable.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: And when you're writing a script processor, you try to keep it as simple as possible

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: because certainly in the 50s and 60s, the thing that interprets the script had to be

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: a very small program because it had to fit in a very small part of memory.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: And so saying, oh, just look at each character.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: And if you see a dollar sign, you jump to another section of the code and then you

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: gobble up characters, say, until the next space or something.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: And you say that's the variable name.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: And so it was sort of invented as a clever way to make parsing of things that contain

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: both variable and fixed parts very easy in a very simple script processor.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: It also helps even then, it also helps the human author and the human reader of the

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: script to quickly see, oh, 20 lines down in the script, I see a reference to X, Y, Z.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Oh, it has a dollar in front of it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: So now we know that X, Y, Z must be one of the parameters of the script.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Well, this is fascinating.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Several things to say, which is the leftovers from the simple script processor languages

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: are now in code bases like behind Facebook or behind most of the back end.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: I think PHP probably still runs most of the back end of the internet.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Oh yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: I think there's a lot of it in Wikipedia too, for example.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: It's funny that those decisions are not funny.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: It's fascinating that those decisions permeate through time.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Just like biological systems, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: I mean, the inner workings of DNA have been stable for, well, I don't know how long it

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: was, like 300 million years.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Half a billion years.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: And there are all sorts of weird quirks there that don't make a lot of sense if you were

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: to design a system like self-replicating molecules from scratch.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Well, that system has a lot of interesting resilience.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: It has redundancy that results, like it messes up in interesting ways that still is resilient

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: when you look at the system level of the organism.
