body.input: did you beyond hiring a great team or working with a great team make it faster? What are some ideas

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: that makes it faster? It has to do with simplicity of software versus performance.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: And so even though C is known to be a low-level language, which is great for writing sort of

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: a high-performance language interpreter, when I originally started Python or CPython, I

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: didn't expect there would be great success and fame in my future. So I tried to get something

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: I tried to get something working and useful in about three months. And so I sort of I cut corners.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: I borrowed ideas left and right when it comes to language design as well as implementation.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: And I also wrote much of the code as simple as it could be. And there are many things that you can

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: code more efficiently by adding more code. It's a bit of a sort of a time-space trade-off

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: where you can compute a certain thing from a small number of inputs. And every time you get presented

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: with a new input, you do the whole computation from the top. That can be simple looking code.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: It's easy to understand. It's easy to reason about that you can tell quickly that it's correct,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: at least in the sort of mathematical sense of correct. Because it's implemented in C,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: maybe it performs relatively well. But over time, as sort of as the requirements for that code and

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: the need for performance go up, you might be able to rewrite that same algorithm you can write in

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: the same algorithm using more memory, maybe remember previous results so you don't have to

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: recompute everything from scratch. Like the classic example is computing prime numbers.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Like is 10 a prime number? Well, you sort of is it divisible by two? Is it divisible by three?

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Is it divisible by four? And we go all the way to is it divisible by nine? And it is not, well,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: actually 10 is divisible by two, so there we stop. Let's say 11 is divisible by 10. The answer is

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: no, 10 times in a row. So now we know 11 is a prime number. On the other hand, if we already know

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: that two, three, five, and seven are prime numbers, and you know a little bit about the mathematics of

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: how prime numbers work, you know that if you have a rough estimate for the square root of 11,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: you don't actually have to check is it divisible by four or is it divisible by five. All you have

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: to check in the case of 11 is is it divisible by two, is it divisible by three? Because take 12,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: if it's divisible by four, well, 12 divided by four is three, so you should have come across

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: the question is it divisible by three first. So if you know basically nothing about prime numbers

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: except the definition, maybe you go for x from two through n minus one is n divisible by x.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: And then at the end, if you got all nos for every single one of those questions,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: you know, oh, it must be a prime number. Well, the first thing is you can stop iterating when

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: you find a yes answer. And the second is you can also stop iterating when you have reached

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: the square root of n, because you know that if it has a divisor larger than the square root,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: it must also have a divisor smaller than the square root. Then you say, oh, except for two,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: we don't need to bother with checking for even numbers because all even numbers are divisible

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: by two. So if it's divisible by four, we would already have come across the question is it

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: divisible by two. And so now you go special case check is it divisible by two, and then you just

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: check three, five, seven, 11. And so now you've you sort of reduced your search space by 50% again by

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: skipping all the even numbers except for two. If you think a bit more about it, or you just

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: read in your book about the history of math, one of the first algorithms ever written down,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: all you have to do is check is it divisible by any of the previous prime numbers that are smaller

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: than the square root. And before you get to a better algorithm than that,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: you have to have several PhDs in discrete math. So that's as much as I know.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: So of course, that same story applies to a lot of other algorithms. String matching is a good

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: example of how to come up with an efficient algorithm. And sometimes the more efficient

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: algorithm is not so much more complex than the inefficient one, but that's an art and it's not

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: always the case. In the general cases, the more performant the algorithm,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: the more complex it's going to be. There's a kind of trade off.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: The simpler algorithms are also the ones that people invent first, because when you're looking

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: for a solution, you look at the simplest way to get there first. And so if there is a simple

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: solution, even if it's not the best solution, not the fastest or the most memory efficient or whatever,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: a simple solution, and simple is fairly subjective, but mathematicians have also

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: thought about sort of what is a good definition for simple in the case of algorithms.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: But the simpler solutions tend to be the most efficient.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: The simpler solutions tend to be easier to follow for other programmers who haven't made a study of

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: a particular field. And when I started with Python, I was a good programmer in general.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: I knew sort of basic data structures. I knew the C language pretty well, but there were many areas

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: where I was only somewhat familiar with the state of the art. And so I picked, in many cases,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: the simplest way I could solve a particular sub-problem, because when you're designing and

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: implementing a language, you have to like, you have many hundreds of little problems to solve.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: And you have to have solutions for every one of them before you can sort of say,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: I've invented a programming language.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: First of all, so C Python, what kind of things does it do? It's an interpreter.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: It takes in this readable language that we talked about that is Python. What is it supposed to do?

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: The interpreter, basically, it's sort of a recipe for understanding recipes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: So instead of a recipe that says, bake me a cake, we have a recipe for, well, given the text of a

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: program, how do we run that program? And that is sort of the recipe for building a computer.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: The recipe for the baker and the chef.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Yeah. What are the algorithmically tricky things that happen to be low hanging fruit

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: that could be improved on? Maybe throughout the history of Python, but also now, how is it

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: possible that 3.11 in year 2022, it's possible to get such a big performance improvement?

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: We focused on a few areas where we still felt there was low hanging fruit.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: The biggest one is actually the interpreter itself. And this has to do with details of

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: how Python is defined. So I don't know if the fisherman is going to follow this story.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: He already jumped off the boat. He's this. I'm bored. This is stupid.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Python is actually, even though it's always called an interpreted language, there's also

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: a compiler in there. It just doesn't compile to machine code. It compiles to bytecode, which is

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: sort of code for an imaginary computer that is called the Python interpreter.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: So it's compiling code that is more easily digestible by the interpreter or is digestible

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: at all. It is the code that is digested by the interpreter. That's the compiler. We tweaked

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: very minor bits of the compiler. Almost all the work was done in the interpreter because

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: when you have a program, you compile it once and then you run the code a whole bunch of times.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Or maybe there's one function in the code that gets run many times. Now I know that

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: sort of people who know this field are expecting me to at some point say,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: we built a just-in-time compiler. Actually, we didn't. We just made the interpreter a little

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: more efficient. What's a just-in-time compiler?

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: That is a thing from the Java world, although it's now applied to almost all

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: programming languages, especially interpreted ones.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: So you see the compiler inside Python, not like a just-in-time compiler, but it's a compiler that

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: creates bytecode that is then fed to the interpreter. And the compiler, was there something

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: interesting to say about the compiler? It's interesting that you haven't changed that,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: tweaked that at all, or much. We changed some parts of the bytecode,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: but not very much. And so we only had to change the parts of the compiler where we decided that

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: the breakdown of a Python program in bytecode instructions had to be slightly different.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: But that didn't gain us the performance improvements. The performance improvements were

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: making the interpreter faster in part by removing the fat from some internal data structures used

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: by the interpreter. But the key idea is an adaptive specializing interpreter.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Let's go. What is adaptive about it? What is specialized about it?

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Well, let me first talk about the specializing part, because the adaptive part is the sort of

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: the second order effect, but they're both important. So bytecode is a bunch of machine

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: instructions, but it's an imaginary machine. But the machine can do things like call a function,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: add two numbers, print a value. Those are sort of typical instructions in Python.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: And if we take the example of adding two numbers, actually in Python, the language,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: there's no such thing as adding two numbers. There's just an

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: the compiler doesn't know that you're adding two numbers. You might as well be adding two strings

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: or two lists or two instances of some user defined class that happen to implement this

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: operator called add. That's a very interesting and fairly powerful mathematical concept.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: It's mostly a user interface trick because it means that

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: a certain category of functions can be written using a single symbol, the plus sign,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: and sort of a bunch of other functions can be written using another single symbol, the multiply sign.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: So if we take addition, the way traditionally in Python, the add bytecode was executed is

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: pointers, pointers, and more pointers. So first, we have two objects. An object is basically a

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: pointer to a bunch of memory that contains more pointers. Pointers all the way down.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Well, not quite, but there are a lot of them. So to simplify a bit, we look up in one of the objects

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: what is the type of that object and does that object type define an add operation?

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: And so you can imagine that there is a sort of a type integer that knows how to add itself to

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: another integer and there is a type floating point number that knows how to add itself

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: to another floating point number. So that's a very interesting thing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: So there is a type integer that knows how to add itself to another floating point number.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: And the integers and floating point numbers are sort of important, I think,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: mostly historically because in the first computers, you used the sort of the same bit pattern when

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: interpreted as a floating point number had a very different value than when interpreted as an integer.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Can I ask a dumb question here?

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Please do.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Given the basics of int and float and add, who carries the knowledge of how to add two integers?

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Is it the integer?

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: It's the type integer versus?

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: It's the type integer and the type float.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: What about the operator? Does the operator just exist as a platonic form possessed by the integer?

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: The operator is more like it's an index in a list of functions that the integer type defines.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: And so the integer type is really a collection of functions and there is an add function and

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: there's a multiply function and there are like 30 other functions for other operations. There's a

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: power function, for example. And you can imagine that in memory there is a distinct slot for the

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: add operations. Let's say the add operation is the first operation of a type and the multiply is the

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: second operation of a type. So now we take the integer type and we take the floating point type.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: In both cases, the add operation is the first slot and multiply is the second slot. But

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: each slot contains a function and the functions are different because the add to integers function

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: interprets the bit patterns as integers. The add to float function interprets the same bit pattern

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: as a floating point number. And then there is the string data type which again interprets the

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: bit pattern as the address of a sequence of characters. There are lots of lies in that story

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: but that's sort of a basic idea.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: I can tell. I can tell the fake news and the fabrication going on here at the table.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: But where's the optimization? Is it on the operator? Is it the different inside the integer?

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: The optimization is the observation that in a particular line of code,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: so now you write your little Python program and you write a function and that function

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: sort of takes a bunch of inputs and at some point it adds two of the inputs together.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Now I bet you even if you call your function a thousand times that all those calls are likely

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: all going to be about integers because maybe your program is all about integers. Or maybe

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: on that particular line of code where there's that plus operator,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: every time the program hits that line the variables a and b that are being added together happen to be

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: strings. And so what we do is instead of having this single byte code that says here's an add

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: operation and the implementation of add is fully generic. It looks at the object from the object,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: it looks at the type, then it takes the type and it looks at the string. And then it takes the

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: type, then it takes the type and it looks at looks up the function pointer, then it calls the function.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Now the function has to look at the other argument and it has to double check that the other argument

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: has the right type. And then there's a bunch of error checking before it can actually

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: just go ahead and add the two bit patterns in the right way. What we do is

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: every time we execute an add instruction like that, we keep a little note of

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: in the end after we hit the code that did the addition for a particular type, what type was it?

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: And then after a few times through that code, if it's the same type all the time,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: we say, oh, so this add operation, even though it's the generic add operation,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: it might as well be the add integer operation. And add integer operation is much more efficient

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: because it just says assume that A and B are integers, do the addition operation,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: do it right there in line and produce the result. So we have to do that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Produce the result. And the big lie here is that in Python, even if you have great evidence that

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: in the past it was always two integers that you were adding, at some point in the future,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: that same line of code could still be hit with two floating points or two strings or maybe a string

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: and an integer. It's not a great lie. That's just the fact of life. I didn't account for what should

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: happen in that case in the way I told the story. There is some accounting for that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: And so what we actually have to do is when we have the add integer operation,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: we still have to check are the two arguments in fact integers. We applied some tricks to make

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: those checks efficient. And we know statistically that the outcome is almost always yes, they are

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: both integers. And so we quickly make that check and then we proceed with the add integer operation.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: And then there is a fallback mechanism where we say, oops, one of them wasn't an integer.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Now we're going to pretend that there was just the fully generic add operation. We wasted a few

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: cycles believing it was going to be two integers and then we had to back up. But we didn't waste

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: that much time and statistically most of the time, basically we were sort of hoping that most of the

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: time we guessed right. Because if it turns out that we guessed wrong too often or we didn't have a good

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: guess at all, things might actually end up running a little slower. So someone with aren't with this

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: knowledge and a copy of the implementation, someone could easily construct a counter example

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: where they say, oh, I have a program and now it runs five times as slow in Python 3.11 than it did

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: in Python 3.10. But that's a very unrealistic program. That's just like an extreme fluke.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: It's a fun reverse engineering task though. So there's a, people like fun. Yes. So there's some

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: presumably heuristic of what defines the momentum of saying, you seem to be working adding two

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: integers, not two generic types. So how do you figure out that heuristic? I think that the heuristic

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: is actually, we assume that the weather tomorrow is going to be the same as the weather today.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: So you don't need two days of the weather? No. That is already so much better than

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: guessing randomly. So how do you find this idea? Hey, I wonder if instead of adding two

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: generic types, we start assuming that the weather tomorrow is the same as the weather today.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Where do you find the idea for that? Because that ultimately, for you to do that, you have to kind

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: of understand how people are using the language, right? Python is not the first language to do a

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: thing like this. This is a fairly well-known trick, especially from other interpreted languages that

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: had reason to be sped up. We occasionally look at papers about HHVM, which is for Facebook's

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: efficient compiler for PHP. There are tricks known from the JVM and sometimes it just comes from

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: academia. So the trick here is that the type itself doesn't, the variable doesn't know what type it is.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: So this is not a statically typed language where you can afford to have a shortcut to saying it's

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: ints. This is a trick that is especially important for interpreted languages with dynamic typing,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: because if the compiler could read in the source, these x and y that we're adding are integers,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: the compiler can just insert the single add machine code, that hardware machine instruction that exists

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: on every CPU and ditto for floats. But because in Python, you don't generally declare the types of

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: your variables, you don't even declare the existence of your variables. They just spring

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: into existence when you first assign them, which is really cool and helps those beginners because

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: there is less bookkeeping they have to learn how to do before they can start playing around with

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: code. But it makes the interpretation of the code less efficient. And so we're trying to

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: make the interpretation more efficient without losing the super dynamic nature of the language.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: That's always the challenge. 3.5 got the PEP 484 type hints. What is type hinting? And is it used

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: by the interpreter, the hints, or is it just syntactic sugar? So the type hints is an optional

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: mechanism that people can use. And it's especially popular with sort of larger companies that have

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: very large code bases written in Python. Do you think of it as almost like documentation saying

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: these two variables are this type? More than documentation. I mean, so it is a sub language

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: of Python where you can express the types of variables. So here is a variable that you can

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: write. And it's an integer. And here's an argument to this function. And it's a string. And here is a

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: function that returns a list of strings. But that's not checked when you run the code.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Exactly. There is a separate piece of software called a static type checker that reads all your

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: source code without executing it and thinks long and hard about what it looks from just reading

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: the code that code might be doing and double checks if that makes sense if you take the types

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: as annotated into account. So this is something you're supposed to run as you develop?

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: It's like a linter. Yeah. That's definitely a development tool. But the type annotations

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: currently are not used for speeding up the interpreter. And there are a number of reasons.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Many people don't use them. Even when they do use them, they sometimes contain lies where

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: the static type checker says everything's fine. I cannot prove that this integer is ever not

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: an integer, but at runtime somehow someone manages to violate that assumption. And the

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: interpreter ends up doing just fine. If we started enforcing type annotations in Python,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: many Python programs would no longer work. And some Python programs wouldn't even be possible

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: because they're too dynamic. And so we made a choice of not using the annotations. There

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: is a possible future where eventually three, four, five releases in the future, we could start using

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: those annotations to sort of provide hints because we can still say, well, the source code leads us

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: to believe that these X and Y are both integers. And so we can generate an add integer instruction

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: but we can still have a fallback that says, oh, if somehow the code at runtime provided something

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: else, maybe it provided two decimal numbers, we can still use that generic add operation as a fallback.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: But we're not there. Is there currently a mechanism or do you see something like that

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: where you can almost add like an assert inside a function that says, please check that my type

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: hints are actually mapping to reality. Sort of like insert manual static typing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: There are third party libraries that are in that business.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Is it possible to do that kind of thing? Is it possible for a third party library to take a hint

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: and enforce it? It seems like a tricky thing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Well, what we actually do is, and I think this is a fairly unique feature in Python,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: the type hints can be introspective at runtime. So while the program is running,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: they mean Python is a very introspectable language. You can look at the variable and ask yourself,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: what is the type of this variable? And if that variable happens to refer to a function,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: you can ask, what are the arguments to the function? And nowadays you can also ask,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: what are the type annotations for the function? So the type annotations are there inside the

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: variable as it's at runtime. They're mostly associated with the function object,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: not with each individual variable, but you can sort of map from the arguments to the variables.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: And that's what a third party library can help with.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Exactly. And the problem with that is that all that extra runtime type checking

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: is going to slow your code down instead of speed it up.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: I think to reference this sales pitchy blog post that says 75% of developers time is spent on

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: debugging, I would say that in some cases that might be okay. It might be okay to pay the cost

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: of performance for the catching of the types, the type errors.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: And in most cases, doing it statically before you ship your code to production

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: is more efficient than doing it at runtime piecemeal.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: I gotta say. Just that part of the world.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: I guess people have nothing better to do in those long, cold winters.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: would you recommend TypeScript or JavaScript? I would recommend TypeScript. Just because of
