body.input: the strictness of the typing. It's an enormously helpful extra tool that helps you sort of

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: keep your head straight about what your code is actually doing. I mean, it helps with editing

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: your code. It helps with ensuring that your code is not too incorrect. And it's actually

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: quite compatible with JavaScript. Never mind this syntactic sort of hack that is still years in the

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: future, but any library that is written in pure JavaScript can still be used from TypeScript

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: programs. And also the other way around, you can write a library in TypeScript and then export it

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: in a form that is totally consumable by JavaScript. That sort of compatibility is

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: sort of the key to the success of TypeScript. Yeah, just to look at it is almost like a

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: biological system that's evolving. It's fascinating to see JavaScript evolve the way it does.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Well, maybe we should consider that biological systems are just engineering systems too, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Yes. Just very advanced with more history. But it's almost like the most visceral in the

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: JavaScript world because there's just so much code written in JavaScript that for its history was

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: messy. If you talk about bugs per line of code, I just feel like JavaScript eats the cake or

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: whatever the terminology is. It beats Python by a lot in terms of the number of bugs, meaning way

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: more bugs in JavaScript. And then obviously the browsers are developing. There's so much

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: active development. It feels a lot more like evolution where a bunch of stuff is born and

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: dies and there's experimentation and debates versus Python. All that stuff is happening,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: but there's just a longer history of stable working giant software systems written in Python

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: versus JavaScript is just a giant, beautiful, I would say mess of code.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: It's a very different culture. To some extent, differences in culture are random, but to some

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: extent, the differences have to do with the environment. And the fact that JavaScript is

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: primarily the language for developing web applications, especially the client side,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: and the fact that it's basically the only language for developing web applications

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: makes that community just have a different nature than the community of other languages.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Plus the graphical component and the fact that they're deploying it on all kinds of shapes of

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: screens and devices and all that kind of stuff, it just creates a beautiful chaos. Anyway, back to

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: MyPy. You talked about a syntax that could work. Where does it currently stand? What's the future

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: static typing in Python? It is still controversial, but it is much more accepted than when MyPy and

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: PEP 484 were young. What's the connection between PEP 484 type hints and MyPy? MyPy

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: was the original static type checker. MyPy quickly evolved from Yuka's own variant of Python to

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: a static type checker for Python. And PEP 484, that was a very productive year where

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: many hundreds of messages were exchanged debating the merits of every aspect of that PEP.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: MyPy is a static type checker for Python. It is itself written in Python. Most additional

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: static typing features that we introduced in the time since 3.6 were also prototyped through MyPy.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: MyPy being an open source project with a very small number of maintainers,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: was successful enough that people said this static type checking stuff for Python is actually worth

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: an investment for our company. But somehow they chose not to support making MyPy faster, say,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: or adding new features to MyPy. But both Google and Facebook and later Microsoft

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: developed their own static type checker. I think Facebook was one of the first

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: they decided that they wanted to use the same technology that they had successfully used for

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: HHVM. Because they had a bunch of compiler writers and static type checking experts

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: who had written the HHVM compiler and it was a big success within the company.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: And they had done it in a certain way. They wrote a big, highly parallel application in an obscure

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: language named OCaml, which is apparently mostly very good for writing static type checkers.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Interesting. I have a lot of questions about how to write a static type checker then.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: That's very confusing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Facebook wrote their own static type checkers.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: And they worked on it in secret for about a year and then they came clean and went open source.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Google, in the meantime, was developing something called PyType, which was mostly

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: interesting because it, as you may have heard, they have one gigantic monorepo.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: So all the code is checked into a single repository.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Facebook has a different approach. So Facebook developed Pyre, which was written in OCaml,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: which worked well with Facebook's development workflow.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Google developed something they called PyType, which was actually itself written in Python.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: And it was meant to sort of fit well in their style of work.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: It was meant to sort of fit well in their static type checking needs in Google's gigantic monorepo.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: So Google has one giant... Got it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Just to clarify, the static type checker, philosophically, is a thing that's supposed

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: to exist outside of the language itself. And it's just a workflow, like a debugger for the...

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: It's a linter.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: For people who don't know, a linter, maybe you can correct me.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: But it's a thing that runs through the code continuously,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: pre-processing to find issues based on style, documentation. I mean, there's all kinds of

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: linters, right? It can check that. What usual things does a linter do? Maybe check that you

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: have too many characters in a single line.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Linters often do static analysis where they try to point out things that are likely mistakes,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: but not incorrect according to the language specification.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Maybe you have a variable that you never use. For the compiler, that is valid.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: You might be planning to use it in a future version of the code, and the compiler might

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: just optimize it out. But the compiler is not going to tell you, hey, you're never using this

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: variable. A linter will tell you that variable is not used. Maybe there's a typo somewhere,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: or else we are you meant to use it, but you accidentally use something else. Or there are

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: a number of common scenarios. A linter is often a big collection of little heuristics,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: where by looking at the combination of how your code is laid out, maybe how it's indented,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: maybe the comment structure, but also just things like definition of names, use of names,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: it'll tell you likely things that are wrong. In some cases, linters are really style checkers.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: For Python, there are a number of linters that check things like,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: do you use the PEP 8 recommended naming scheme for your functions and classes and variables?

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Because classes start with an uppercase, and the rest starts with a lowercase.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: There are slight differences there. The linter can tell you, hey, you have a class whose

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: first letter is not an uppercase letter. I just find it annoying if I wanted that to be an

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: uppercase letter. I would have typed an uppercase letter, but other people find it very comforting

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: that if the linter is no longer complaining about their code, that they have followed all the style

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: rules. Maybe it's a fast way for a new developer joining a team to learn the style rules, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Yeah, there's definitely that. But the best use of a linter is probably not so much to sort of

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: enforce team uniformity, but to actually help developers catch bugs that the compilers,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: for whatever reason, don't catch. There's lots of that in Python.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: A static type checker focuses on a particular aspect of the linting, which,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: I mean, my pi doesn't care how you name your classes and variables, but it is meticulous

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: about when you say that there was an integer here and you're passing a string there, it will tell

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: you, hey, that string is not an integer. So something's wrong. Either you were incorrect

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: when you said it was an integer or you're incorrect when you're passing into string.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: If this is a race of static type checkers, is somebody winning? Is this a race of static

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: linting? As you said, it's interesting that the companies didn't choose to invest in this

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: centralized development of my pi. Is there a future for my pi? What do you see as that?

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Will one of the companies win out and everybody uses like a pi type, whatever Google's is called?

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Well, Microsoft is hoping that Microsoft's horse in that race called Pi Right is going to win.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Pi Right, right, like R-I-G-H-T.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Correct. Yeah, all my word processors tend to typo correct that as Pi Right, the name of the,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: I don't know what it is, some kind of semi-precious metal.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Oh, right. I love it. Okay. So, okay, that's the Microsoft hope, but okay, so let me ask the

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: question a different way. Is there going to be ever a future where the static type checker gets

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: integrated into the language? Nobody is currently excited about doing any work towards that. That

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: doesn't mean that five or 10 years from now, the situation isn't different. At the moment,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: all the static type checkers still evolve at a much higher speed than Python and its annotation

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: syntax evolve. You get a new release of Python once a year. Those are the only times that you

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: can introduce new annotation syntax. And there are always people who invent new annotation

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: syntax that they're trying to push. And worse, once we've all agreed that we are going to put

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: some new syntax in, we can never take it back. At least the sort of deprecating an existing feature

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: takes many releases because you have to assume that people started using it as soon as we

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: announced it. And then you can't take it away from them right away. You have to start telling

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: them, well, this will go away, but we're not going to tell you that it's an error yet. And then later

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: it's going to be a warning. And then eventually three releases in the future, maybe we remove it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: On the other hand, the typical static type checker still has a release like

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: every month, every two months, certainly many times a year. Some type checkers are

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: some type checkers also include a bunch of experimental ideas that aren't official standard

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Python syntax yet. The static type checkers also just get better at discovering things that

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: are unspecified by the language, but that could make sense. And so each static type checker actually

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: has its sort of strong and weak points. So it's cool. It's like a laboratory of experiments.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Yeah. Microsoft, Google and all, and you get to see. And you see that everywhere, right? Because

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: there's not one single JavaScript engine either. There is one in Chrome, there is one in Safari,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: there is one in Firefox. But that said, you said there's not interest. I think

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: that there is a lot of interest in type hinting, right? In the PEP 484. Actually,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: like how many people use that? Do you have a sense how many people use, because it's optional,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: it's a sugar. I can't put a number on it, but from the number of packages that do interesting

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: things with it at runtime and the fact that there are like now three or four very mature type

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: checkers that each have their segment of the market. And then there's PyCharm, which has

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: a sort of more heuristic based type checker that also supports the same syntax. My assumption is

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: that many, many people developing Python software professionally for some kind of production

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: situation are using a static type checker. Especially anybody who has a continuous integration

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: cycle probably has one of the steps in their testing routine that happens for basically every

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: commit is run a static type checker. And in most cases, that will be MyPy.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: So I think it's pretty popular topic. According to this webpage, 20 to 30% of Python 3 code bases

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: are using type hints. Wow. I wonder how they measured that. Did they just scan all of GitHub?

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Yeah, that's what it looks like. They did a quick set, not all of, but like a random sampling.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: So you mentioned PyCharm. Let me ask you the big subjective question. What's the best IDE for

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Python? And you're extremely biased now that you're with Microsoft. Is it PyCharm VS code Vim or Emacs?

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Historically, I actually started out with using Vim, but when it was still called VI,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: for a very long time, I think from the early 80s to, I'd say, two years ago, I was Emacs user.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Nice. Between, I'd say 2013 and 2018, I dabbled with PyCharm, mostly because of the

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: features. I mean, PyCharm is like driving an 18-wheeler truck, whereas Emacs is more

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: like driving your comfortable Toyota car that you've had for 100,000 miles and you know what

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: every little rattle of the car means. But I think it's a very good example of that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: I was very comfortable in Emacs, but there were certain things it couldn't do. It wasn't very

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: good at that sort of, at least the way I had configured it. I didn't have very good tooling

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: in Emacs for finding the definition of a function. When I was at Dropbox exploring a 5 million line

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341
