body.input: that if you grab all 5 million lines of code, there are many classes with the same name.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: So PyCharm, once you fired it up and once it's indexed, your repository was very helpful.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: But as soon as I had to edit code, I would jump back to Emacs and do all my editing there because

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: I could type much faster and switch between files when I knew which file I wanted much quicker.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: And I never really got used to the whole PyCharm user interface.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Yeah, I feel torn in that same kind of way because I've used PyCharm off and on exactly

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: in that same way. And I feel like I'm just being an old grumpy man for not learning how to quickly

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: switch between files and all that kind of stuff. I feel like that has to do with shortcuts,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: that has to do with, I mean, you just have to get accustomed just like with touch typing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Yeah, you have to just want to learn that. I mean, if you don't need it much,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: you don't need touch typing either. You can type with two fingers just fine in the short term,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: but in the long term, you're looking for a little bit of a more complex way to do it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: So you can do it in the short term, but in the long term, your life will become better

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: psychologically and productivity wise if you learn how to type with 10 fingers.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: If you do a lot of keyboard input.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: But for everyone, emails and stuff, right? Like you look at the next 20, 30 years of your life,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: you have to anticipate where technology is going. Do you want to invest in handwriting notes?

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: More and more people are doing typing versus handwriting notes. So you can anticipate that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: So there's no reason to actually practice handwriting. There's more reason to practice

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: typing. You can actually estimate back to the spreadsheet, the number of paragraphs,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: sentences or words you write for the rest of your life.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: You could probably go again with the spreadsheet of my life.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Yes. All of that is not actually converted to a spreadsheet, but the gut feeling.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: I have the same kind of gut feeling about books. I've almost exclusively switched to Kindle now,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: for ebook readers, even though I still love and probably always will the smell,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: the feel of a physical book. The reason I switched to Kindle is like, all right,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: well, this is really paving the future is going to be digital in terms of consuming

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: books and content of that nature. So you should let your brain get accustomed to that experience.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: And that same way, it feels like PyCharm or VS code. I think PyCharm is the most sophisticated,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: featureful Python ID. It feels like I should probably at some point very soon switch entirely.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: I'm not allowed to use anything else for Python than this ID or VS code. It doesn't matter,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: but walk away from Emacs for this particular application. So I think I'm limiting myself

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: in the same way that using two fingers for typing is limiting myself.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: This is a therapy session. I'm not even asking questions.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: But I'm sure a lot of people are thinking this way.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: I'm not going to stop you. I think that everybody has to decide for themselves

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: which one they want to invest more time in. I actually ended up giving VS code a very tentative

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: try when I started out at Microsoft and really liking it. It took me a while before I realized

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: why that was. I think that actually the founders of VS code may not necessarily agree with me on

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: this. But to me, VS code is in a sense the spiritual successor of Emacs. Because as you probably know

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: as an old Emacs hack, the key part of Emacs is that it's mostly written in Lisp. That sort of

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: new features of Emacs usually update all the Lisp packages and add new Lisp packages.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: And oh yeah, there's also some very obscure thing improved in the part that's not in Lisp,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: but that's usually not why you would upgrade to a new version of Emacs. There's a core

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: implementation that can read a file and it can put bits on the screen and it can manage memory and

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: buffers. And then what makes it an editor full of features is all the Lisp packages. And of course,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: the design of how the Lisp packages interact with each other and with that base layer of the core

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: immutable engine. But almost everything in that core engine in Emacs case can still be overridden

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: or replaced. And so VS code has a similar architecture where there is like a base engine

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: that you have no control over. I mean, it's open source, but nobody

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: really accepts the people who work on that part. It changes it much. And it has a sort of a package

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: manager and a whole series of interfaces for packages and an additional series of

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: conventions for how packages should interact with the lower layers and with each other.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: And powerful primitive operations that let you move the cursor around or select pieces of text

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: or delete pieces of text or interact with the keyboard and the mouse and whatever peripherals

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: you have. And so the extreme extensibility and the package ecosystem that you see in VS code

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: is a mirror of very similar architectural features in Emacs.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Well, I'll have to give it a serious try because as far as sort of the hype and the excitement

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: in the general programming community, VS code seems to dominate. The interesting thing about

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: PyCharm and what is it, PHP Storm, which are these JetBrains specific IDs that are designed

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: for one programming language, it's interesting to, when an ID is specialized, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: They're usually actually just specializations of IntelliJ because underneath it's all the same

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: editing engine with different veneer on top, where in VS code, many things you do require

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: loading third party extensions. In PyCharm, it is possible to have third party extensions,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: but it is a struggle to create one.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Yes, and it's not part of the culture, all that kind of stuff.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Yeah, I remember that might have been five years ago or so we were trying to get some

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: better MyPy integration into PyCharm because MyPy is sort of Python tooling and PyCharm

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: had its own type checking heuristic thing that we wanted to replace with something based on MyPy

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: because that was what we were using in the company. For the guy who was writing that PyCharm

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: extension, it was really a struggle to sort of find documentation and get the development workflow

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: going and debug his code and all that. That was not a pleasant experience.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Let me talk to you about parallelism. In your post titled, reasoning about async IOS semaphore,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: you talk about a fast food restaurant in Silicon Valley that has only one table. Is this a real

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: thing? I just wanted to ask you about that. Is that just like a metaphor you're using or is that an

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: actual restaurant in Silicon Valley?

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: It was a metaphor, of course.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: I can imagine such a restaurant. For people who don't, then read the thing you should.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: It was an idea of a restaurant where there's only one table and you show up one at a time

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: and you're prepared. I actually looked it up and there is restaurants like this throughout the world.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: It just seems like a fascinating idea. You stand in line, you show up, there's one table,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: they ask you all kinds of questions, they cook just for you. That's fascinating.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: It sounds like you'd find places like that in Tokyo. It sounds like a very Japanese thing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Or in the Bay Area, there are pop-up places that probably more or less work like that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: I've never eaten at such a place.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: The fascinating thing is you propose as a fast food. This is all for a burger.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: It was one of my rare sort of more literary or poetic moments where I thought I'll just

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: open with a crazy example to catch your attention. The rest is very dry stuff about locks and

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: semaphores and how a semaphore is a generalization of a lock.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: It was very poetic and well delivered. It actually made me wonder if it's real or not

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: because you don't make that explicit. It feels like it could be true. In fact, I wouldn't be

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: surprised if somebody listens to this and knows exactly a restaurant like this in Silicon Valley.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Anyway, can we step back and can you just talk about parallelism, concurrency, threading,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: asynchronous, all of these different terms? What is it at a high philosophical level?

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: The fisherman is back in the boat.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Well, the idea is if the fisherman has two fishing rods, since fishing is mostly a matter

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: of waiting for a fish to nibble. Well, it depends on how you do it actually. If you're

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: doing the style of fishing where you throw it out and then you let it sit for a while

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: until maybe you see a nibble, one fisherman can easily run two or three or four fishing

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: rods. As long as you can afford the equipment, you can catch four times as many fish by

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: small investment in four fishing rods. Since your time, you say you have all Saturday to go fishing,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: if you can catch four times as much fish, you have a much higher productivity.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: That's actually I think how deep sea fishing is done. You could just have a rod and you

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: put in a whole thing, you could have many rods. You can catch a lot of fish,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: you can catch many rods. Is there an interesting difference between parallelism and concurrency

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: and asynchronous? Is there one subset of the other to you? How do you think about these terms?

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: In the computer world, there is a big difference. When people are talking about parallelism,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: like a parallel computer, that's usually really several complete CPUs that are sort of tied

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: together and share something like memory or an IO bus. Concurrency can be a much more abstract

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: concept where you have the illusion that things happen simultaneously, but what the computer

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: actually does is it spends a little time running this program for a while and then it spends some

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: time running that program for a while and then spending some time for the third program for a

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: while. So parallelism is the reality and concurrency is part reality, part illusion.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Yeah, parallelism typically implies that there is multiple copies of the hardware.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: You write that implementing synchronization primitives is hard in that blog post and you

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: talk about locks and semaphores. Why is it hard to implement synchronization primitives?

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Because at the conscious level, our brains are not trained to sort of keep track of multiple things

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: at the same time. Obviously, you can walk and chew gum at the same time because they're both

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: activities that require only a little bit of your conscious activity, but try balancing your checkbook

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: and watching a murder mystery on TV. You'll mix up the digits or you'll miss an essential clue

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: in the TV show. So why does it matter that the programmer, the human, is bad?

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Because the programmer is, at least with the current state of the art, is responsible for

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: writing the code correctly and it's hard enough to keep track of a recipe that you just

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: execute one step at a time. Chop the carrots, then peel the potatoes, mix the icing. You need

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: your whole brain when you're reading a piece of code, what is going on? Okay, we're loading

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: the number of mermaids in variable A and the number of mermen in variable B and now we take

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: the average or whatever. I like how we're just jumping from metaphor to metaphor. I like it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: You have to keep in your head what is in A, what is in B, what is in C. Hopefully, you have better

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: names and that is challenging enough. If you have two different pieces of code that are sort of

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: being executed simultaneously, whether it's using the parallel or the concurrent approach, if A is

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: the number of fishermen and B is the number of programmers, but in another part of the code,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: A is the number of mermaids and B is the number of mermen. And somehow that's the same variable.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: If you do it sequentially, if first you do your mermaid, merpeople computation and then you do

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: your people in the boat computation, it doesn't matter that the variables are called A and B and

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: that is literally the same variable because you're done with one use of that variable. But

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: when you mix them together, suddenly the number of merpeople replaces the number of fishermen and

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: your computation goes dramatically wrong. And there's all kinds of ordering of operations

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: that could result in the assignment of those variables. And so you have to anticipate all

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: possible orderings. And you think you're smart and you'll put a lock around it. And in practice,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: in terms of bugs per line of per thousand lines of code, this is an area where everything is worse.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: So a lock is a mechanism by which you forbid only one chef can access the oven at a time.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Something like that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: And then semaphores allow you to do what? Multiple ovens?

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: That's not a bad idea because if you're sort of, if you're preparing, if you're baking cakes and

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: you have multiple people all baking cakes, but there's only one oven, then maybe you can tell

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: that the oven is in use, but maybe it's preheating. And so you have to, maybe you make a sign that

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: says oven in use and you flip the sign over and it says oven is free when you're done baking your

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: cake. That's a lock. And what do you do when you have two ovens or maybe you have 10 ovens?

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: You can put a separate sign on each oven or maybe you can sort of someone who can put a sign on each

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: oven or maybe you can sort of someone who comes in wants to see at a glance and maybe there's an

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: electronic sign that says there are still five ovens available or maybe there are already three

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: people waiting for an oven. So you can, if you see an oven that's not in use, it's already reserved

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: for someone else who got in line first. And that's sort of what the restaurant metaphor was trying to

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: explain. Yeah. And so you're now tasks you're sitting as a designer of Python with a team of

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: brilliant core developers and have to try to figure out to what degree can any of these ideas be

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: integrated and not. So maybe this is a good time to ask what is async IO and how has it evolved

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: since Python 3.4? Wow. Yeah. So we had this really old library for doing things concurrently,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: especially things that had to do with IO and networking IO was especially a sort of a popular

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: topic. And in the Python standard library, we had a brief period where there was lots of development

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: and I think it was late nineties, maybe early two thousands and like two little modules were added

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: that were the state of the art of doing asynchronous IO or sort of non-blocking IO,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: which means that you can keep multiple network connections open and sort of service them all in

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: parallel like a typical web server does. So IO is input and outputs, you're writing either to

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: the network or reading from a network connection or reading and writing to a hard drive, storage.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Also possible. And you can do the ideas you could do to multiple while also doing computation.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: So running some code that does some fancy stuff. Yeah. Like when you're writing a web server,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: when a request comes in, a user sort of needs to see a particular web page.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: You have to find that page maybe in the database and format it properly and send it back to the

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: client. And there's a lot of waiting, waiting for the database, waiting for the network. And so you

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: can handle hundreds or thousands or millions of requests concurrently on one machine. Anyway,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: ways of doing that in Python were kind of stagnated. And I forget, it might've been around

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: 2012, 2014 when someone for the umpteenth time actually said these async chat and async core

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: modules that you have in a standard library are not quite enough to solve my particular problem.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Can we add one tiny little feature? And everybody said, no, that stuff is not to,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: you're not supposed to use that stuff. Write your own using a third party library. And then everybody

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: started a debate about what the right third party library was. And somehow I felt that

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: there was actually a cue for, well, maybe we need a better state of the art module in the standard

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: library for multiplexing input output from different sources. You could say that it spiraled

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: out of control a little bit. It was at the time, it was the largest Python enhancement proposal

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: that was ever proposed. And you were deeply involved with that. At the time, I was very

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: much involved with that. I was like the lead architect. I ended up talking to people who had

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: already developed serious third party libraries that did similar things and sort of taking ideas

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: from them and getting their feedback on my design. And eventually we put it in the standard library.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: And after a few years, I got distracted. I think the thing, the big thing that distracted me was

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: actually type annotations. But other people kept it alive and kicking and it's been quite successful

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: actually in the world of Python web clients. So initially, what are some of the design challenges

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: there in that debate for the PEP? And what are some things that got rejected? What are some things

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: that got accepted to stand out to you? There are a couple of different ways you can handle parallel

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: IO. And this happens sort of at an architectural level in operating systems as well. Like Windows

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: prefers to do it one way and Unix prefers to do it the other way. You sort of, you have an object

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: that represents a network endpoint, say a connection with a web browser that your client,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: and say you're waiting for an incoming request. Two fundamental approaches are

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: okay, I'm waiting for an incoming request. I'm doing something else. Come wake me up or

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: sort of come tell me when something interesting happened, like a packet came in on that network

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: connection. And the other paradigm is we're on a team of a whole bunch of people with maybe a little

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: mind and we can only manage one web connection at a time. So we're on a team of a whole bunch

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: of people. I'm just sitting looking at this web connection and I'm just blocked until something

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: comes in and then I'm already waiting for it. I get the data, I process the data and then I go

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: back to the top and say, no, sort of I'm waiting for the next packet. Those are about the two

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: paradigms. One is a paradigm where there is sort of notionally a thread of control, whether it's an

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: actual operating system thread or more an abstraction in async IO, we call them tasks.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: But a task in async IO or a thread in other contexts is devoted to one thing and it has logic

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: for all the stages. When it's a web request, first wait for the first line of the web request,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: parse it because then you know if it's a get or a post or a put or whatever or an error.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Then wait until you have a bunch of lines until there's a blank line, then parse that as headers

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: and then interpret that and then wait for the rest of the data to come in if there is any more that

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: you expect, that sort of standard web stuff. The other thing is, and there's always endless

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: debate about which approach is more efficient and which approach is more error prone, where I just

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: have a whole bunch of stacks in front of me and whenever a packet comes in, I sort of look at the

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: number of the packet, that there's some number on the packet and I say, oh, that packet goes on this

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: pile and then I can do a little bit and then sort of that pile provides my context. And as soon as

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: I'm done with the processing, I sort of, I can forget everything about what's going on because

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: the next packet will come in from some random other client and it's that pile or this pile.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: And every time a pile is maybe empty or full or whatever the criteria is, I can toss it away or

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: use it for a new space. But several traditional third party libraries for asynchronous I-O

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: processing in Python shows the model of a callback. And that's the idea where you have a bunch of

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: different stacks of paper in front of you and every time someone gives you a piece, gives you

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: a new sheet, you decide which stack it belongs to. And that leads to a certain style of spaghetti code

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: that I find sort of aesthetically not pleasing and I was sort of never very successful and I

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: had heard many stories about people who were also sort of complaining about that style of coding.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: It was very prevalent in JavaScript at the time at least because it was like how the JavaScript

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: event loop basically works. And so I thought, well, the task-based model where each task has

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: a bunch of logic, we had mechanisms in the Python language that we could easily reuse for that. And

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: I thought I want to build a whole library for asynchronous networking I-O and all the other

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: things that may need to be done asynchronously based on that paradigm. And so I just chose a

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: paradigm and tried to see how far I could get with that. And it turns out that it's a pretty good

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: paradigm. So people enjoy that kind of paradigm programming for asynchronous I-O relative to

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: callbacks. Okay, beautiful. So how does that all interplay with the infamous GIL, the Global

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Interpreter Lock? Maybe can you say what the GIL is and how does it dance beautifully with asynchronous

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: I-O? The Global Interpreter Lock solves the problem that Python originally was not written

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: with either asynchronous or parallelism in mind at all. There was no concurrency in the language.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: There was no parallelism. There were no threads. Only a small number of years into Python's initial

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: development, all the new cool operating systems like SunOS and Silicon Graphics, IRIX, and then

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: eventually POSIX and Windows all came with threading libraries that let you do multiple things in

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: parallel. And there is a certain sort of principle, which is the operating system handles the threads

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: for you. And the program can pretend that there are as many CPUs as there are threads in the program.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: And those CPUs work completely independently. And if you don't have enough CPUs, the operating

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: system sort of simulates those extra CPUs. On the other hand, if you have enough CPUs,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: you can get a lot of work done by deploying those multiple CPUs. But Python wasn't written

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: to do that. And so as libraries for multi-threading were added to C, but every operating system vendor

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: was adding their own version of that, we thought, and maybe we were wrong, but at the time we thought,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: well, we quickly want to be able to do that. And so we started to think about how we could

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: quickly want to be able to support these multiple threads because they seemed at the time in the

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: early 90s when they were new, at least to me, they seemed a cool, interesting programming paradigm.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: And one of the things that Python, at least at the time, felt was nice about the language was

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: that we could give a safe version of all kinds of cool new operating system toys to the Python

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: programmer. I remember one or two years before threading, I had spent some time adding networking

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: sockets to Python. And there were very literal translation of the networking sockets that were

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: in the BSD operating system, so Unix BSD. But the nice thing was if you were using sockets from

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Python, then all the things you can do wrong with sockets in C would automatically give you a clear

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: error message instead of just ending up with a malfunctioning hanging program. And so we thought,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: well, we'll do the same thing with threading. But we didn't really want to rewrite the interpreter

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: to be thread safe because that would be a very complex refactoring of all the interpreter code

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: and all the runtime code because all the objects were written with the assumption that there's

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: only one thread. And so we said, okay, well, we'll take our losses, we'll provide something that

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: looks like threads. And as long as you only have a single CPU on your computer, which most computers

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: at the time did, it feels just like threads because the whole idea of multiple threads in the OS was

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: that even if your computer only had one CPU, you could still fire up at many threads as you wanted.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Well, within reason, maybe 10 or 12, not 5,000. And so we thought we had conquered the

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: abstraction of threads pretty well because multi-core CPUs were not in most Python programmers'

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: hands anyway. And then of course, a couple of more iterations of Moore's law and computers

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: getting faster. And at some point, the chip designers decided that they couldn't make the

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: CPUs faster, but they could still make them smaller. And so they could put multiple CPUs

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: on one chip. And suddenly there was all this pressure about do things in parallel. And that's

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: where the solution we had in Python didn't work. And that's sort of the moment that the GIL became

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: infamous. Because the GIL was the solution we used to take this single interpreter and share it

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: between all the different operating system threads that you could create. And so as long as the

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: hardware physically only had one CPU, that was all fine. And then as hardware vendors were suddenly

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: telling us all, oh, you got to paralyze. Everything's got to be paralyzed. People started saying,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: oh, but we can use multiple threads in Python. And then they discovered, oh, but actually all

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: threads run on a single core. Yeah. Is there a way, is there ideas in the future to remove

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: the global interpreter law GIL? Like maybe... It's a very good question.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: ...multiple sub-interpreters, some tricky interpreters on top of interpreters kind of thing?

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Yeah, there are a couple of possible futures there. The most likely future is that we'll get

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: multiple sub-interpreters, which each run a completely independent Python program.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Nice. But there's still some benefit of faster communication between those programs.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: But it's also managing for you this running a multiple Python programs. So it's hidden from

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: you, right? It's hidden from you, but you have to spend more time communicating between those

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: programs because the sort of the attractive thing about the multi-threaded model is that the threads

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: can share objects. At the same time, that's also the downfall of the multi-threaded programming model

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: because when you do share objects, and you didn't necessarily intend to share them or

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: there were aspects of those objects that were not reusable, you get all kinds of concurrency bugs.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: The reason I wrote that little blog post about semaphores was that concurrency bugs are just

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: harder. It would be nice if Python had no global interpreter lock and it had the so-called free

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: threading, but it would also cause a lot more software bugs. The interesting thing is that

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: there is still a possible future where we could experiment at least with that because there's a

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: guy working for Facebook who has developed a fork of CPython that he called the no-gil

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: interpreter where he removed the gil and made a whole bunch of optimizations so that the

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: single-threaded case doesn't run too much slower and multi-threaded case will actually

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: use all the cores that you have. That would be an interesting possibility if we would be willing,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: as Python core developers, to actually maintain that code indefinitely and if we're willing to

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: put up with the additional complexity of the interpreter and the additional overhead for

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: the single-threaded case. I'm personally not convinced that there are enough people needing

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: the speed of multiple threads with their Python programs that it's worth to take that

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Speaking of packages, they have a lot of impact on a lot of people's lives. Does it make sense

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: permeated the entire data science, machine learning, AI community?

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: road, which you have to do for safety reasons. You have to agree on something. They could have

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: picked JavaScript or Perl. There was a time in the early 2000s that it really looked like Perl was

body.input: going to dominate like biosciences because DNA search was all based on regular expressions,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: and Perl has the fastest and most comprehensive regular expression engine, still does.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: I spent quite a long time with Perl. That was another letting go of this kind of data processing

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: system. The reasons why Python became the lingua franca of scientific

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: code and machine learning in particular and data science, it really had a lot to do with

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: anything was better than C or C++. Recently, a guy who worked at Lawrence Livermore National

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Laboratories in the computing division wrote me his memoirs and he had his own view of how he helped

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: something he called computational steering into existence. This was the idea that you take libraries

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: that in his days were written in Fortran that solved universal mathematical problems,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: and those libraries still work, but the scientists that used the libraries used them to solve

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: continuously different specific applications and answer different questions. Those poor scientists

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: were required to use, say, Fortran because Fortran was the language that the library was written in,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: and then the scientist would have to write an application that uses the library to solve a

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: particular equation or answer a set of questions. The same for C++. There's interoperability,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: so the dusty decks are written either in C++ or Fortran. Paul Dubois was one of the people who,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: I think, in the mid-90s saw that you needed a higher level language for the scientists

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: to tie together the fundamental mathematical algorithms of linear algebra and other stuff.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Gradually, some libraries started appearing that did very fundamental stuff with arrays of numbers

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: in Python. When I first created Python, I was not expecting it to be used for arrays of numbers

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: much. I thought that was an outdated data type, and everything was like objects and strings,

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: and Python was good and fast at string manipulation and objects, obviously, but arrays of numbers

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: were not very efficient, and the multi-dimensional arrays didn't even exist in the language at all.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: But there were people who realized that Python had extensibility that was flexible enough that they

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: could write third-party packages that did support large arrays of numbers and operations on them

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: very efficiently. Somehow, they got a foothold through different parts of the scientific

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: community. I remember that the Hubble Space Telescope people in Baltimore were somehow big

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Python fans in the late 90s. At various points, small improvements were made, and more people

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: got in touch with using Python to derive these libraries of interesting algorithms.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Once you have a bunch of scientists who are working on similar problems, say they're all

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: working on data that comes in from the Hubble Space Telescope, but they're looking at different

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: things. Some are looking at stars in this galaxy, others are looking at galaxies in the other.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: The math is completely different, but the underlying libraries are still the same.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: And so they exchange code. They say, well, I wrote this Python program, or I wrote a Python

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: library to solve this class of problems. And the other guys either say, oh, I can use that library

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: too, or if you make a few changes, I can use that library too. Why start from scratch?

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: Why start from scratch in Perl or JavaScript where there's not that infrastructure

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: for arrays of numbers yet? Whereas in Python, you have it. And so more and more scientists

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: at different places doing different work discovered Python. And then people who had an idea for an

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: important new fundamental library decided, oh, Python is actually already known to our users.

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: So let's use Python as the user interface. I imagine at least that's how TensorFlow ended

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

body.input: up with Python as the user interface. Right. But with TensorFlow, there's a

metadata.title: Podcast: Guido van Rossum: Python and the Future of Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #341

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeremy Howard: fast.ai Deep Learning Courses and Research | Lex Fridman Podcast #35

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeremy Howard: fast.ai Deep Learning Courses and Research | Lex Fridman Podcast #35

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeremy Howard: fast.ai Deep Learning Courses and Research | Lex Fridman Podcast #35

body.input: For sure, yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeremy Howard: fast.ai Deep Learning Courses and Research | Lex Fridman Podcast #35

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeremy Howard: fast.ai Deep Learning Courses and Research | Lex Fridman Podcast #35

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeremy Howard: fast.ai Deep Learning Courses and Research | Lex Fridman Podcast #35

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeremy Howard: fast.ai Deep Learning Courses and Research | Lex Fridman Podcast #35

body.input: Yeah, I mean, funnily enough, the problem

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeremy Howard: fast.ai Deep Learning Courses and Research | Lex Fridman Podcast #35

body.input: is less the regulation and more the interpretation

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeremy Howard: fast.ai Deep Learning Courses and Research | Lex Fridman Podcast #35

body.input: of that regulation by lawyers in hospitals.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeremy Howard: fast.ai Deep Learning Courses and Research | Lex Fridman Podcast #35

body.input: So HIPAA was actually designed to be,

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeremy Howard: fast.ai Deep Learning Courses and Research | Lex Fridman Podcast #35

body.input: and HIPAA does not stand for privacy.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeremy Howard: fast.ai Deep Learning Courses and Research | Lex Fridman Podcast #35

body.input: And it was created with lots of gray areas

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeremy Howard: fast.ai Deep Learning Courses and Research | Lex Fridman Podcast #35

body.input: because the idea is that would be more practical

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeremy Howard: fast.ai Deep Learning Courses and Research | Lex Fridman Podcast #35

body.input: and would help people to use this legislation to actually

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeremy Howard: fast.ai Deep Learning Courses and Research | Lex Fridman Podcast #35

body.input: share data in a more thoughtful way.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeremy Howard: fast.ai Deep Learning Courses and Research | Lex Fridman Podcast #35

body.input: Unfortunately, it's done the opposite

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeremy Howard: fast.ai Deep Learning Courses and Research | Lex Fridman Podcast #35

body.input: because when a lawyer sees a gray area,

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeremy Howard: fast.ai Deep Learning Courses and Research | Lex Fridman Podcast #35

body.input: they see, oh, if we don't know, we won't get sued,

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeremy Howard: fast.ai Deep Learning Courses and Research | Lex Fridman Podcast #35

body.input: then we can't do it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeremy Howard: fast.ai Deep Learning Courses and Research | Lex Fridman Podcast #35

body.input: So HIPAA is not exactly the problem.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeremy Howard: fast.ai Deep Learning Courses and Research | Lex Fridman Podcast #35

body.input: The problem is more that hospital lawyers are not

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeremy Howard: fast.ai Deep Learning Courses and Research | Lex Fridman Podcast #35

body.input: incented to make bold decisions about data portability.

body.input: Or even to embrace technology that saves lives.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeremy Howard: fast.ai Deep Learning Courses and Research | Lex Fridman Podcast #35

body.input: They more want to not get in trouble

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeremy Howard: fast.ai Deep Learning Courses and Research | Lex Fridman Podcast #35

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeremy Howard: fast.ai Deep Learning Courses and Research | Lex Fridman Podcast #35

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeremy Howard: fast.ai Deep Learning Courses and Research | Lex Fridman Podcast #35

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeremy Howard: fast.ai Deep Learning Courses and Research | Lex Fridman Podcast #35

body.input: But it's like, which ones were helped?

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeremy Howard: fast.ai Deep Learning Courses and Research | Lex Fridman Podcast #35

body.input: It's very abstract.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeremy Howard: fast.ai Deep Learning Courses and Research | Lex Fridman Podcast #35

body.input: And on the conner side of that, you

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeremy Howard: fast.ai Deep Learning Courses and Research | Lex Fridman Podcast #35

body.input: But on the question of privacy, data

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeremy Howard: fast.ai Deep Learning Courses and Research | Lex Fridman Podcast #35

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeremy Howard: fast.ai Deep Learning Courses and Research | Lex Fridman Podcast #35

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeremy Howard: fast.ai Deep Learning Courses and Research | Lex Fridman Podcast #35
